Ken Kovach built a decades-long career in organizational development, leadership training, and community service. Drawing on advanced study in sociology, he worked as a coach, consultant, educator, and facilitator for businesses, government agencies, nonprofits, and national programs, including serving for ten years as lead facilitator for NASA’s “Linking Leaders” initiative.

In Cleveland, Kovach held leadership roles with Case Western Reserve University’s Mandel Center for Nonprofit Organizations, United Way Services, the International Services Center, the International Community Council, and numerous civic organizations. He also served more than 21 years on Shaker Heights City Council and taught at several Northeast Ohio colleges and universities.

His civic work extended internationally, particularly through long-term educational and management partnerships in Russia. He also helped strengthen Cleveland’s international communities, including supporting the establishment of the India Cultural Garden. For decades, he served as Choirmaster and Ecclesiarch at St. Theodosius Cathedral.

Kovach’s work brought together education, civic leadership, faith, international exchange, and cross-cultural understanding—earning recognition from organizations in Cleveland and abroad.

Milton Maltz built a national career in broadcasting, philanthropy, and cultural institution-building. He founded Malrite Communications Group in 1956 and led it for more than four decades, growing the company into a major operator of radio and television stations across the United States.

His connection to broadcasting began early. As a child, Maltz acted in radio dramas in Chicago and later appeared in some of television’s earliest broadcasts. He went on to work in news, production, management, and industry leadership. He also wrote, produced, and directed “The Fight for Freedom,” a radio drama series about the creation of the State of Israel.

Maltz became an influential voice in the broadcast industry, creating the National Association of Broadcasters’ Task Force for Free TV and serving in leadership roles with several national media organizations. His achievements earned him recognition in the broadcasting Hall of Fame and the University of Cincinnati’s Frederic W. Ziv Award for outstanding achievement in telecommunications.

In Cleveland, Maltz helped shape the region’s cultural landscape. He was instrumental in bringing the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and Museum to the city. With his wife, Tamar, he also founded the Maltz Museum of Jewish Heritage in Beachwood, creating a place to explore Jewish history, immigration, identity, and the experiences of Northeast Ohio’s diverse communities.

His philanthropy has supported many Cleveland institutions, including the Cleveland Orchestra, Case Western Reserve University, Cleveland Play House, the Jewish Federation of Cleveland, the Anti-Defamation League, Israel Bonds, and the Cleveland Clinic Foundation. His support also extended to medical research and charitable organizations around the country.

Maltz brought his experience in media and entertainment to other major cultural projects. He helped develop the International Spy Museum in Washington, D.C., served on the Board of the CIA Officers Memorial Foundation, and, with Tamar Maltz, revived a regional theater in Jupiter, Florida, that became the Maltz Jupiter Theatre.

Across broadcasting, museums, the arts, education, healthcare, and philanthropy, Milton Maltz helped build institutions designed to inform, entertain, and bring people together. His impact on Cleveland is especially visible in the cultural organizations he helped create, support, and strengthen.

Mary Rose Oakar built a public-service career that stretched from Cleveland classrooms and City Council to the Ohio legislature and the United States Congress. Born and raised in Cleveland, she earned a B.A. from Ursuline College and an M.A. from John Carroll University, with additional study in England and at Cleveland-Marshall College of Law. Before entering politics, she taught at East High School, Lourdes Academy, Ursuline College, and Cuyahoga Community College.

Oakar first entered public office on Cleveland City Council, serving from 1973 to 1976. In 1976, she was elected to Congress, where she represented Cleveland and surrounding communities for 16 years. She later served in the Ohio House of Representatives and on the Ohio State Board of Education. Her career connected neighborhood concerns in Cleveland with state, national, and international public policy.

In Congress, Oakar became part of the House Democratic leadership and held influential committee assignments involving banking, housing, aging, and government administration. Public housing and community development were particular concerns from the beginning of her congressional career. She also became known for work on women’s economic equality, cancer prevention and screening, healthcare, aging, and drug and alcohol treatment and prevention.

Her work on health and social issues brought recognition from organizations including the American Cancer Society, Susan G. Komen Foundation, Consumer Federation of America, Alliance for Aging Research, National Association for Homecare, and organizations representing addiction-treatment professionals. President Bill Clinton later appointed her to the advisory board for the White House Conference on Aging.

Oakar also gave particular attention to immigrants, ethnic communities, civil rights, and Cleveland’s international connections. She received recognition from the American Nationalities Movement and Nationalities Service Center for her work with immigrant communities. After leaving Congress, she served for more than six years as national president of the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee, working on civil rights, hate crimes, racial profiling, and civil liberties in coalition with other national organizations.

Her international work extended to Central Europe and the Middle East. Oakar served as a U.S. parliamentarian with NATO, participated in election-monitoring efforts in Palestinian territories and Czechoslovakia, and was appointed to the Builders for Peace initiative supporting economic development in the Middle East. She attended major Middle East peace events during the Clinton administration and participated in delegations connected with the peace process.

Education remained another constant throughout her career. In addition to her earlier teaching, Oakar taught government, English, speech, and drama at institutions across Northeast Ohio, including Cuyahoga Community College, Cleveland State University, and Ursuline College. She also lectured nationally and hosted television and radio programs focused on current affairs and issues affecting older adults.

Across education, local government, Congress, civil rights, health policy, and international affairs, Mary Rose Oakar carried Cleveland experiences into national public life. Her career linked the city’s neighborhoods and immigrant communities with debates over housing, healthcare, aging, equality, and America’s role in the wider world.

Vladimir Rus was born in Rijeka, Croatia, in 1925 and later settled in Cleveland after living in Croatia and Trieste. He earned a Ph.D. in Political Science from the University of Trieste and pursued advanced study at Western Reserve University and the University of Michigan.

In Cleveland, Rus became a major interpreter of Eastern European and Slavic history. He taught at Cuyahoga Community College, Cleveland State University, and Western Reserve University, offering courses on Yugoslavia, Slovenia, Slavic languages, and Greater Cleveland’s ethnic communities. At Tri-C, he also coordinated the Inter-Cultural Relations program and taught a course on Cleveland’s urban challenges with Mayor Ralph Perk.

His most concrete civic impact came through workforce development. At Cuyahoga Community College, Rus helped redesign labor-studies and apprenticeship programs, developed training for displaced workers, and led the Urban Metropolitan Development Institute, which connected the college’s educational resources directly to Cleveland’s economic-development needs.

Through the United Labor Agency, he worked with the AFL-CIO, Teamsters, and United Auto Workers and helped establish the Cleveland Area Labor-Management Council. He also developed federally funded training programs, including one that prepared unemployed, out-of-school youth for building-maintenance work at Cleveland Metropolitan Housing Authority properties.

Rus later served as Cleveland’s Director of Human Resources and Economic Development, where he helped coordinate job training, workforce policy, and economic-development planning across the Cleveland-area labor market.

He also strengthened Cleveland’s international ties. As President of the Cleveland/Ljubljana Sister Cities Committee and the Slovenian American Heritage Foundation, a charter member of the Slovenian American Business Council, and a leader with the International Services Center, Rus connected Cleveland’s Slovenian and immigrant communities to the city’s civic institutions and international partnerships.

Across classrooms, labor programs, City Hall, and cultural organizations, Vladimir Rus helped Cleveland respond to economic change while preserving and strengthening the immigrant communities that shaped the city.

Dr. Shah’s greatest impact in Greater Cleveland has been her ability to turn medical expertise into organized community action. After more than 30 years as a pediatrician, she continued serving Northeast Ohio as a volunteer physician at the Painesville Free Clinic, providing care to families with limited access to healthcare.

Within Cleveland’s Indian American community, Shah became a major humanitarian organizer. As Chair of the Association of Indian Physicians of Northern Ohio’s Humanitarian Services Committee, she brought together physicians, volunteers, donors, and civic partners for medical and relief efforts locally and overseas.

She also helped establish Community Helping Hands with Mona Alag, Gita Gidwani, Kamala Nagpal, and other local leaders. The organization built a network of more than 50 volunteers across Greater Cleveland to assist Indian and immigrant families facing domestic violence, medical emergencies, terminal illness, legal problems, deportation crises, and the challenges faced by new immigrants and students.

Shah used these Cleveland-based professional and volunteer networks to extend the region’s impact internationally. With her husband, Ramesh Shah, she organized Medical YATRA teams of physicians and volunteers from the United States, United Kingdom, and Canada. Over seven years, the program provided medical assistance to more than 100,000 rural villagers in India.

Her humanitarian work included 27 medical camps across 10 countries and seven Indian states, as well as missions to Mexico, Haiti, the Dominican Republic, Uganda, Kenya, and India. She helped organize responses to the Gujarat earthquake, Indian Ocean tsunami, Hurricane Katrina, disasters in Mexico, and the 2010 Haiti earthquake. She also joined an American Red Cross delegation to Kenya as part of a measles-eradication initiative.

The medical camps provided primary care and free medicines while raising funds for treatments patients could not otherwise afford. Programs included “Gift of Sight” cataract surgeries and “Gift of Heart,” which helped provide pacemakers, stents, and heart valves in India. Rotary grants also supported several of these missions.

In Cleveland, Shah’s lasting legacy is the network she helped create—linking physicians, immigrant organizations, volunteers, and families into a practical system of medical service, crisis assistance, and humanitarian action that reached from Northeast Ohio to communities around the world.

Anthony Yen built a career connecting Cleveland businesses and institutions to markets across Asia and the wider world. Through decades of work in international trade, manufacturing, education, and civic leadership, he helped strengthen Cleveland’s position in the global economy.

Yen played a central role in Cleveland’s international business community. He served with the Cleveland World Trade Association, Greater Cleveland Growth Association, Northern Ohio District Export Council, and World Trade Center Cleveland, where he was an advisor and chaired its Education Foundation. He was also appointed to the Governor of Ohio’s Advisory Council on International Trade and became a longtime member of the Ohio Commodores Association.

As a businessman and consultant, Yen developed extensive commercial ties between the United States and Asia. He led or advised companies operating in Cleveland, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, China, and elsewhere, including Yen Enterprises, International Equipment Sales and Consulting, Universeas Corporation, Universal Engineering, and ABC International. His consulting work included relationships with major Asian industrial groups such as Yulon Motor and Hyundai.

Yen also helped organize and participate in international trade missions to Europe, China, Japan, Korea, Taiwan, and Southeast Asia. In 1987, he helped organize the Small Business Administration’s first trade mission to the People’s Republic of China, as well as trade missions to Japan, Korea, and Taiwan. His work brought Cleveland-area businesses into direct contact with international markets and helped introduce regional companies to opportunities abroad.

He represented Cleveland and Ohio at trade conferences throughout the United States and internationally, speaking in cities including Taipei, Osaka, Paris, Beijing, and Shanghai. He also participated in the White House Conference on International Trade and addressed universities, government organizations, business associations, and international economic forums.

Yen extended this global work into Cleveland’s educational and cultural institutions. He served on advisory boards and committees at Cleveland State University, Case Western Reserve University, the Cleveland Institute of Art, the Cleveland Clinic, the University of Akron, and Hathaway Brown School. He later chaired the Board of Trustees of Cleveland State University’s Confucius Institute and served on the university’s College of Education and Human Resources Visiting Committee.

From 2002 to 2009, Yen produced and hosted “Asian Hour” on WERE 1490 Radio One, creating another connection between Cleveland’s Asian communities and the wider region.

His contributions received recognition from business and government organizations in the United States and abroad. Honors included Cleveland’s International Business Executive of the Year, the Cleveland World Trade Association’s Ambassador to the International Trade Community award, federal and state awards for excellence in exporting, recognition for decades of service to the U.S. Department of Commerce District Export Council, and Taiwan’s Brilliant Star Award, First Class. In 2011, Cleveland State University awarded him an honorary Doctor of Education degree.

Anthony Yen’s Cleveland legacy is the international network he helped build around the city—linking local businesses, universities, government agencies, and Asian communities to global markets and institutions. His work helped make international trade and cross-cultural exchange a practical part of Cleveland’s economic and civic life.

John “Jack” P. Coyne built long careers in law, business, and civic leadership in Cleveland. A Cleveland native and graduate of Benedictine High School, he earned degrees in accounting and law from the University of Notre Dame. He served eight years as a Captain in the U.S. Army and Ohio National Guard and practiced law in Cleveland for more than five decades.

Coyne founded Park-Here, Inc., later known as Coyne-Kangesser Parking and eventually part of ABM, where he served as Vice President of Development. He became widely known in the parking industry, serving as a Director of the National Parking Association and a Trustee of the Cleveland Parking Association. He also served on the boards of the Historic Warehouse District and Downtown Cleveland Alliance and held legal and leadership roles with several Northeast Ohio savings and loan institutions.

His civic involvement included leadership with the St. Ignatius Fathers’ Club, Catholic Counseling Center, University of Notre Dame–Cleveland Club, and other community organizations. His strongest and most lasting legacy, however, grew from more than six decades of involvement in Cleveland’s Irish American community.

Coyne became active in that community at age 17, serving as Drum Major for the East Side Irish American Club before later becoming involved with the West Side Irish American Club. There he worked with labor leader and Irish activist Terry Joyce, an association that led Coyne to the Irish National Caucus. Founded by Father Sean McManus during the conflict in Northern Ireland, the Caucus sought to give Irish American concerns a stronger voice in Washington. Coyne became president of its Cleveland chapter.

That work led directly to Project Children. The program brought Catholic and Protestant children from Northern Ireland to the United States for summers away from sectarian violence and the influence of paramilitary groups. Cleveland welcomed its first group in 1983, and Coyne took charge of the local program the following year. He and his wife, Mary, personally organized interviews, host-family placements, summer activities, and fundraising. The Cleveland chapter continued until 1996.

Coyne also helped make Irish history a permanent part of Cleveland’s public landscape. As a founding member of the Irish Famine Committee, he helped create the city’s Irish Famine Memorial, dedicated on September 16, 2000, along with a time capsule preserving the community’s history.

He later became a founding member and four-year president of the Irish American Political Action Committee, which supported Irish American participation in local and national politics. That organization evolved into the Irish American Charitable Foundation, where Coyne served as president. The Foundation provided support for Irish cultural and educational projects across Northeast Ohio.

Its work included bringing the Irish Sopranos to Severance Hall, supporting renovation and expansion of the Irish Cultural Garden, helping Cleveland Public Theatre present a tribute to W. B. Yeats, and underwriting the republication of the Greater Cleveland Irish Directory.

Coyne’s lasting Cleveland legacy is the civic and cultural infrastructure he helped build around Irish American life. Through Project Children, the Famine Memorial, cultural organizations, philanthropy, and decades of community leadership, he helped preserve Irish heritage while connecting it to peace-building, public life, and the broader story of Cleveland.

The Most Reverend Anthony Edward Pevec devoted more than five decades to Catholic education, parish life, and church leadership in Greater Cleveland. Born in Cleveland in 1925, he attended St. Vitus Elementary School and Cathedral Latin High School before preparing for the priesthood at Sacred Heart Seminary and St. Mary Seminary. He earned a master’s degree from John Carroll University and a Ph.D. from Western Reserve University.

Ordained a priest in 1950, Pevec served first at St. Mary Church in Elyria and St. Lawrence Church in Cleveland. Much of his early career, however, was spent educating future priests and Catholic leaders. From 1953 to 1975, he taught and held increasingly senior leadership positions at Borromeo Seminary High School, serving as teacher, assistant principal, vice-rector, principal, and rector. He also taught graduate courses at St. John College in Cleveland.

Pevec returned to one of Cleveland’s historic Slovenian parishes when he became pastor of St. Vitus Church in 1975. His leadership there connected his ministry directly to the religious and cultural life of Cleveland’s Slovenian community. In 1979, he became Rector-President of Borromeo College of Ohio.

In 1982, Pevec was ordained a bishop and appointed Vicar of the Diocese of Cleveland’s Eastern Region, a position he held until his retirement in 2001. In that role, he helped oversee parish and clergy life across a large portion of the diocese while continuing his involvement in Catholic education and priestly formation.

Pevec also served on numerous diocesan, state, and national committees concerned with vocations, clergy relations, Catholic secondary education, seminary evaluation, pro-life issues, and the relationship between science and human values. His service included leadership with the Catholic Conference of Ohio and committees of the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, as well as chaplain roles with the Catholic Order of Foresters and Knights of Columbus.

His contributions were recognized by both church and community organizations. Honors included Slovenian Man of the Year, induction into the St. Vitus Hall of Fame, Wickliffe Man of the Year, Knights of Columbus Catholic Man of the Year, Cathedral Latin Alumni Association Man of the Year, and recognition from John Carroll University.

Pevec’s Cleveland legacy lies especially in the generations he taught and mentored, the parishes he served, and the connection he maintained between Catholic leadership and Cleveland’s Slovenian American community.
note: Reviewed by Tony Yanick in the staff review app.

Dr. Maria Pujana has built a Cleveland career spanning medicine, public health, philanthropy, international affairs, and the arts. A physician, clinical neurologist, and neurophysiologist, she has served on the faculty of Case Western Reserve University School of Medicine’s Global Health program, bringing medical expertise into broader work on public health and international development.

Her most sustained civic role was with the Cleveland Foundation, where she served on the Board of Directors from 2002 to 2012. She chaired the Foundation’s scholarship advisory and selection committee, helping direct educational opportunities to students, and founded and chaired its International Committee, expanding the Foundation’s engagement with Cleveland’s international communities and global connections.

Pujana also brought her medical and international experience to several major Cleveland institutions. She served on the MetroHealth Foundation Board, chaired the International Affairs and Services Committee of the Cleveland Red Cross, advised the Cleveland Institute of Art, and participated in the Cleveland Office of Minority Health Advisory Committee. These roles placed her at the intersection of healthcare access, humanitarian service, cultural institutions, and the needs of Cleveland’s diverse communities.

Her civic involvement also included Leadership Cleveland’s Class of 2005 and work with the Helen Moss Cancer Research Foundation and Invest in Children. Together, these positions allowed her to contribute directly to scholarship access, healthcare, international outreach, minority health, and arts leadership across the region.

Outside medicine and civic service, Pujana developed Marise Designs, a fine and fashion jewelry company whose work appeared at Madrid’s Pasarela Cibeles Fashion Week and New York Fashion Week and in publications including Vogue, Hola, Latina Style, and The Plain Dealer.

Her work has been recognized with honors including the Distinguished Ohioan Award, TiE Ohio Community Catalyst Award, YWCA Women of Achievement Award, and the Hispanic Business Association Visionary Award.

Pujana’s Cleveland legacy is especially visible in the institutions she helped lead: expanding scholarship opportunities through the Cleveland Foundation, strengthening international engagement through the Foundation and Red Cross, contributing to minority and public health initiatives, and linking Cleveland’s medical, philanthropic, and cultural communities.

Ratanjit S. Sondhe built his Cleveland legacy through entrepreneurship, minority business development, and civic leadership. After emigrating from India in 1968 with two master’s degrees and $8, he continued his studies in polymer chemistry at the University of Akron.

In 1973, Sondhe founded POLY-CARB, Inc., a materials science company he led for 34 years until its acquisition by The Dow Chemical Company in 2007. At POLY-CARB, he developed an unusual management model without traditional titles or bosses, relying instead on shared values, documented operating principles, and individual responsibility.

His most significant Cleveland contribution was launching the Multicultural Business Development Center at the Urban League of Greater Cleveland. Rather than focusing only on placing residents into jobs, Sondhe promoted business ownership and wealth creation as a path to greater economic opportunity for Cleveland’s inner-city communities. The program became influential enough that the National Urban League adopted the model for replication in other cities.

That work connected Sondhe directly to Cleveland’s civil-rights and economic-development landscape and contributed to his 2010 induction into the Ohio Civil Rights Hall of Fame.

He also served on the boards of the Cleveland Foundation, Project Love, the American Red Cross, and the City Club Foundation, contributing to philanthropy, youth development, humanitarian service, and civic dialogue across the region.

Beyond Cleveland, Sondhe became internationally known for his philosophy of “Oneness,” which emphasized leadership from within and stress-free living. Known as “Mr. Stress Free,” he worked as an author, speaker, leadership coach, consultant, and radio and television personality. His television programs reached audiences in more than 150 countries, and he produced more than 800 audio and 600 video programs.

His books included *TEA: The Recipe for Stress-free Living*, *The Secret of Our Ultimate Success*, and *101 Gems to Re-Align Our Lives*. He also developed the leadership program *ZERO—The Core of Leadership*. In 2006, the NRI Institute presented him with the Pride of India Gold Award in London for his international contributions to stress-free living.

In Cleveland, Sondhe’s lasting contribution was using entrepreneurship as a tool for expanding business ownership, economic independence, and wealth-building opportunities in communities historically excluded from them—while carrying ideas developed here to audiences around the world.
note: Reviewed by Tony Yanick in the staff review app.

Andrew Chakalis built a career linking art, education, cultural preservation, and Cleveland’s immigrant communities. A native Clevelander, he attended Brush High School and Case Western Reserve University, where his study of Italian earned him a fellowship to the Academy of Fine Arts in Florence in 1966.

While in Italy, Chakalis worked at the marble quarries of Carrara, ceramic kilns in Faenza, and with sculptor Arnaldo Pomodoro in Milan. He returned to Cleveland in 1970 and joined the Cleveland Museum of Art in 1974.

As Assistant Curator of the museum’s Extensions Division, Chakalis directed a major educational outreach program, organizing exhibitions for more than 100 schools across 35 districts and adapting displays to classroom curricula. He managed a teaching collection of more than 16,000 works spanning Western and Asian art and added roughly 100 objects each year through the Harold T. Clark Education Extension Fund.

His work brought the museum directly into Cleveland-area classrooms. He also organized “Life Images: A Child’s View,” an exchange of drawings between local elementary students and children in Odawara, Japan.

At the museum, Chakalis curated exhibitions that explored Cleveland’s own history, including “Progressive Vision: The Planning of Downtown Cleveland 1903–1930” and “The Age of Elegance: Cleveland 1880–1914.” He also designed exhibition catalogues and contributed to museum publications. In 1988, he lectured at the Taiwan Museum of Art on collections and educational outreach.

One of his most lasting civic contributions grew from the Cleveland Museum of Art exhibition “Holy Image, Holy Space: Icons and Frescoes from Greece.” Chakalis and Helen Collis organized representatives from four local Greek churches to support the exhibition. That committee became the nucleus of the Hellenic Preservation Society of Northeastern Ohio, which Chakalis helped found and served for decades.

After the Extensions Division closed in 1993, he returned full time to sculpture while continuing his cultural work. He served with the Greek Garden Association of Cleveland and received the Friend of India Award for helping establish the India Cultural Garden. He was also recognized by the City of Brook Park and Cleveland Public Library for preserving local cultural heritage.

Chakalis’s Cleveland legacy lies in bringing museum collections into schools, interpreting the city’s history through exhibitions, and helping immigrant communities preserve and share their culture in public life. He was the first person of Greek heritage inducted into the Cleveland International Hall of Fame.
note: Reviewed by Tony Yanick in the staff review app.

Lucy Torres has spent decades strengthening Cleveland’s Puerto Rican and Latino communities through education, cultural leadership, city government, housing, and neighborhood advocacy. Born and raised in Comerío, Puerto Rico, she was shaped by a family tradition of faith, responsibility, and service. She studied nursing at Universidad del Sagrado Corazón before moving to Cleveland in 1978.

In Cleveland, Torres became a trusted connector between families, public institutions, and community organizations. As President and Vice President of the Puerto Rican Parade of Cleveland, she helped sustain and expand one of the city’s most visible expressions of Puerto Rican culture, bringing artists, public figures, and government representatives from Puerto Rico to Cleveland. She also served with the Hispanic American Committee, Julia de Burgos Youth Cultural Center, Club Alma Yaucana, and cultural events including Festival del Café and Festival de la Calle 33.

For 15 years, Torres worked with the Cleveland Metropolitan School District as a liaison between families and the school system. She helped Latino and multilingual parents navigate schools, access services, and connect with educational resources, strengthening relationships between Cleveland families and public education.

From 2006 to 2016, Torres brought that experience into City Hall as a community liaison in Mayor Frank Jackson’s administration. She participated in outreach initiatives across Cleveland and founded the first Mayor’s Advisory Board, creating a direct channel for residents and community leaders to bring concerns, needs, and ideas to city government.

Torres also supported local political campaigns and civic initiatives centered on community advancement. She continued developing her own skills through Cleveland State University, Cuyahoga Community College, Hondros Real Estate Academy, and numerous workshops and conferences focused on serving the Latino community. Her work earned recognition including Cleveland State University’s Sister Alicia Award.

Her public service extended into housing as Leasing Manager at Valley Road Villa, a senior housing community, where she worked until January 2025.

Torres also built her Cleveland life around family. She shared 31 years of marriage with Iván Torres, a community advocate, and continued her public service after his death in 2010. She is the mother of Yaris I. Martínez and grandmother of Christopher Jr., Christian, Kris, and Yariliz.

Lucy Torres’s Cleveland legacy is the civic bridge she helped build between Latino families and the institutions that shape daily life—schools, City Hall, housing, cultural organizations, political life, and public celebrations. Her leadership helped strengthen representation, access, cultural visibility, and civic participation for Cleveland’s Puerto Rican and Latino communities.

For more than four decades, Le Nguyen helped Asian residents navigate immigration, city government, neighborhood life, and cultural change. As a trusted mediator and liaison, he became a bridge between families, organizations, neighborhoods, and City Hall.

Nguyen was born in Can Tho, Vietnam, one of eight siblings. As a young man, he served in security with the South Vietnamese Air Force and rose to the rank of Sergeant. On April 28, 1975, two days before the Fall of Saigon, he survived the bombing of Tan Son Nhut Airport. Soon afterward, he fled Vietnam with his brother and nephew.

By October 1975, Nguyen had resettled in Muskegon, Michigan. Determined to rebuild his life, he attended Indiana Vocational Technical College and earned an associate degree in Electronics and Technology in 1980. Later that year, he moved to Cleveland.

In 1981, Earl Williams Sr. hired Nguyen to assist Vietnamese refugees settling in the city. Over time, Nguyen worked with more than 125 families displaced by war, helping them secure housing, access food assistance, and navigate lawful permanent residency and U.S. citizenship.

His ability to earn trust and solve practical problems led to a 32-year career with the City of Cleveland. His work gained recognition during Mayor George Voinovich’s administration, and he later served as the city’s Asian Liaison under Mayor Michael White. He continued working with Asian residents and organizations through the administrations of Jane Campbell and Frank Jackson.

When disputes arose, newcomers encountered government barriers, or organizations needed help developing programs, Nguyen was often the person called. His work extended beyond City Hall into churches, temples, neighborhood organizations, and individual households, where he mediated conflicts and connected residents with public agencies.

Nguyen also helped make Asian traditions more visible in city life. Working with volunteers, he supported celebrations including the Moon Festival and Lunar New Year, creating opportunities for families to maintain cultural traditions while sharing them with a wider public.

His work was especially important to Cleveland’s Vietnamese population. With Councilman Matt Zone, Nguyen helped establish the Vietnamese Community of Greater Cleveland around Detroit Avenue and West 65th Street. He served as its president from 1990 to 2012, creating a durable base for cultural programming, advocacy, and assistance.

Nguyen retired from city service in 2012 to care for his wife, Bonnie, after she was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. He devoted himself to her care until her death later that year. In 2025, Nguyen faced another personal challenge when he was diagnosed with colon cancer and successfully underwent treatment.

Le Nguyen’s Cleveland legacy is visible in the families he resettled, the Vietnamese institutions he helped establish, and the connections he built between Asian residents and local government. His work made Cleveland easier to navigate for newcomers while creating lasting space for cultural identity, representation, and civic participation.
note: Reviewed by Tony Yanick in the staff review app.

Catherine Jorgensen McCutcheon has spent decades connecting Cleveland to its Scandinavian heritage while also advancing international exchange, immigrant education, safe cycling, and neighborhood advocacy.

In 1993, McCutcheon became one of twelve founding members of the Ohio Norsemen. The organization grew from an effort to commemorate an extraordinary chapter in Cleveland history: the 1893 arrival of the *Viking*, a replica of Norway’s ninth-century Gokstad ship that sailed across the Atlantic for the World’s Columbian Exposition. When the ship reached Cleveland on July 3, thousands gathered along the waterfront to welcome it.

A century later, McCutcheon and the other founders marked the anniversary with an open house aboard the *William G. Mather*. About 400 visitors explored exhibits tracing the *Viking’s* voyage, accompanied by Norwegian food and materials supplied by the Norwegian embassy. Stephen Mulloy’s Cleveland legacy can be found not only in clubs, parades, and formal institutions, but in something more personal: the door he kept open. Pope John Paul II appointed Pilla Auxiliary Bishop of Cleveland in 1979 and named him the ninth Bishop of Cleveland the following year. He was installed on January 6, 1981 and led the Diocese until his retirement in 2006.

His years as bishop coincided with profound changes in Cleveland: population loss, neighborhood disinvestment, suburban growth, economic restructuring, and persistent questions of racial and economic inequality. It placed questions of economic justice, neighborhood life, the environment, and social responsibility within the Church’s public mission.

Pilla’s leadership also reached beyond Northeast Ohio. After serving three years as Vice President of the National Conference of Catholic Bishops, he was elected its President in 1995 and served through 1998. From Cleveland, he became one of the leading institutional voices of the Catholic Church in the United States.

Yet much of his career remained tied to the institutions that had formed him: Cleveland parishes, seminaries, schools, clergy, and neighborhoods. Education and formation remained central themes from his years at Borromeo through his leadership of the entire Diocese.

Bishop Anthony Pilla’s Cleveland legacy lies in widening the idea of what religious leadership could mean for a city. Through seminaries, parishes, civic partnerships, and *Church in the City*, he encouraged Catholics across Northeast Ohio to understand Cleveland’s neighborhoods, inequalities, and future as shared concerns—and made the Diocese an active participant in those conversations.

Jim Craciun has spent decades connecting Cleveland’s Romanian American heritage with human rights, refugee resettlement, neighborhood service, and international cultural life. Born and raised in Cleveland in 1951, he graduated cum laude from St. Edward High School in 1969 and earned a business degree in labor and industrial relations from Cleveland State University in 1973.

In 1976, Craciun became a licensed funeral director and joined the family business. His father and mother had established the Craciun funeral-home tradition in Cleveland, and Jim and his brother Joseph joined the business in the 1970s. Funeral homes bearing the Craciun name have continued serving families across Cleveland, Fairview Park, Middleburg Heights, and Westlake.

Craciun’s Romanian heritage also drew him into international human-rights work. In 1974, he carried Bibles and catechisms into Communist Romania. At an international human-rights conference in London in 1977, he participated in efforts challenging repression in Soviet-bloc countries. Beginning in 1982, he spoke throughout Northeast Ohio on “Life under Communism,” helping local audiences understand conditions behind the Iron Curtain.

In 1984, Craciun became a founding member of the World Union of Free Romanians in Geneva and later served as vice president from 1987 to 2004. His Cleveland International Hall of Fame biography also records that in January 1995 he advised the Clinton administration on NATO enlargement, at a moment when the United States was publicly developing its policy toward expanding the alliance into Central and Eastern Europe.

His civic work in Cleveland was equally broad. Craciun served as President of the West Cleveland Jaycees and West Cleveland Kiwanis and as a board member of West Side Ecumenical Ministry. From 1989 to 1991, he led the Diocesan Union of Holy Name Societies, representing organizations across eight Northeast Ohio counties and 245 churches.

Craciun became especially involved in organizations serving Cleveland’s immigrant and international communities. From 2002 to 2009, he chaired the International Services Center, helping guide an agency that assisted refugees and newcomers establishing lives in Northeast Ohio. He also chaired Cleveland’s International Folk Festivals at Playhouse Square in 2000 and 2001 and co-chaired the Cultural Committee for the 2004 International Children’s Games.

His service also reached deeply into neighborhood institutions. He founded Cub Scout Pack 541 at Our Lady of Mount Carmel School and later served as president of the school foundation. In 2010, he became incorporating secretary of the Cleveland Police Foundation and later served as its vice president. He also contributed to University Hospitals through its ENT Council.

Craciun’s work earned the American Nationalities Movement Freedom Award in 2007 for his contributions to human rights, peace, and civic organizations.

He built this public life alongside his wife, Marcy Rocawich Craciun, and their five children. After Marcy’s death in 2010, his family remained closely connected to both the funeral-home business and his Cleveland civic life.

Jim Craciun’s Cleveland legacy lies in the range of institutions he helped connect: a family business serving local families, Romanian human-rights advocacy, refugee resettlement, international festivals, schools, churches, and civic organizations. His career turned a strong ethnic identity outward—using it not only to preserve Romanian heritage, but to support newcomers and strengthen Cleveland’s wider international community.

Dr. Wael Khoury built a Cleveland career that moved between cardiology, international affairs, Arab American civic leadership, and the Cultural Gardens. His work helped strengthen both the region’s medical institutions and its identity as a city connected to the wider world.

Khoury graduated from the University of Damascus Medical School in 1975 and came to Cleveland for postgraduate training. He completed an internal-medicine residency at Huron and St. Luke’s Hospitals from 1976 to 1979, followed by a cardiology fellowship at Case Western Reserve University and University Hospitals. He became board certified in internal medicine and cardiology and a Fellow of the American College of Cardiology.

Beginning in 1981, Khoury served for more than three decades as President of Cardiology Associates of Cleveland. At Marymount Hospital, he became Head of Cardiology in 1982 and later directed both the cardiac catheterization laboratory and congestive-heart-failure clinic. His administrative leadership included service as Chief of Staff from 1993 to 1995 and Vice President of Medical Affairs from 1995 to 2001.

His work also became integrated into the Cleveland Clinic system. Khoury served as consultant faculty, later joined the Clinic’s cardiology staff, directed clinical research for the system’s eastern region, and participated as principal investigator in numerous cardiology research projects.

Parallel to that medical career, Khoury became increasingly active in Cleveland’s Arab American institutions. He served as First Vice President of the Cleveland American Middle East Organization in the early 1980s and later assumed major leadership roles in the National Arab American Medical Association.

Within NAAMA, Khoury served as Ohio chapter president and advanced through national positions as secretary, vice president, president-elect, and ultimately national president in 2001. His work was not limited to professional medicine. As chair of cultural and Syrian liaison activities, he helped bring leading Arab poets and musicians to Cleveland and participated in medical conventions, seminars, and professional exchanges throughout Syria and other Arab countries.

Khoury also helped create permanent cultural institutions in Cleveland. In 2005, he became the founding president of the Syrian American Cultural Council. Beginning in 2008, he chaired development of the Syrian Cultural Garden, helping give Syrian history, art, and identity a lasting public presence within Rockefeller Park.

His leadership then expanded beyond the Syrian community. In 2017, Khoury became President of the Cleveland Cultural Gardens Federation, working across the organizations representing Cleveland’s many nationality communities. His path from founding a single cultural council to leading the wider Federation reflected a larger commitment to cultural cooperation.

International affairs became another major part of his civic life. Khoury served for years with the Cleveland Council on World Affairs and later chaired its board. He also participated in the Cleveland Committee on Foreign Relations, linking local institutions with discussions of diplomacy, global affairs, and international exchange.

Dr. Wael Khoury’s Cleveland legacy is unusually broad but interconnected. In medicine, he helped build and lead cardiac services serving patients across the region. In civic life, he connected Arab American professionals and artists to Cleveland institutions. Seung “Sam” Kim built his Northeast Ohio life through repeated acts of reinvention—from soldier and machinist to entrepreneur, Korean American civic leader, and advocate for veterans.

Born in South Korea in 1947, Kim served in the South Korean Army during the Vietnam War in 1969, part of the allied Korean forces serving alongside the United States. After completing his military service, he returned home, married Daenam, and began raising a family.

In the 1970s, the family immigrated to the United States in search of greater opportunity. After a brief period in New Jersey, they settled in Warren, Pennsylvania. Kim worked full time while attending school full time and completed a machinist apprenticeship, becoming a licensed master machinist in 1986. During those years, he and his family also became naturalized U.S. citizens.

The family later moved to Erie, where Kim worked for an engineering company while he and Daenam also operated a shoe-repair shop and restaurant. As manufacturing declined across the Rust Belt and industrial jobs became less secure, Kim again changed direction.

Around the beginning of the new millennium, he learned the dry-cleaning trade and established a successful business in Elyria. That move brought him more deeply into Greater Cleveland’s Korean American community.

In 2009, Kim was elected President of the Korean American Association of Greater Cleveland. His leadership emphasized both cultural connection and civic participation, helping Korean American families engage more fully with the wider region.

His experience as a veteran became one of the strongest themes of that work. Kim organized and supported events honoring both Korean and American veterans, bringing together people whose military service connected the two countries. He went on to serve as President of the Korean Vietnam Veterans Ohio Chapter as well as its national organization.

Kim also served as an advisor within the Korean American Association’s Midwest network and as an elder at Ashtabula Korean Church, linking civic leadership with faith and community life.

His cultural involvement extended into Tae Kwon Do. A fifth-degree black belt and Olympic-level referee, Kim helped carry a Korean martial tradition into his American life.

Kim and Daenam raised their family in the United States and became proud grandparents to Gigi and Jack.

Seung “Sam” Kim’s Northeast Ohio legacy reflects the immigrant experience across several generations and industries. He adapted as manufacturing changed, built a business in Elyria, strengthened Korean American institutions, and created lasting ties between Korean and American veterans. His life connected service to one country with citizenship in another—and made both part of his contribution to Greater Cleveland.

William F. “Bill” Miller spent four decades showing Clevelanders just how international their own city was. As a reporter for *The Plain Dealer*, and especially during 15 years writing the “Ethnic Scene” column, he documented the neighborhoods, traditions, organizations, celebrations, and personal stories of Greater Cleveland’s immigrant communities.

Miller’s reporting began with a question he was famous for asking almost anyone he met: “What is your ethnic heritage?” For him, the question was never about placing someone into a category. It was an invitation to learn where people came from, what traditions they carried, and how those histories became part of Cleveland.

He rarely reported from a distance. Miller attended festivals, danced to unfamiliar music, sang along, sampled traditional foods, visited churches and community halls, and listened closely before returning to the newsroom to write. Through his columns, a reader could move from one part of the world to another without leaving Northeast Ohio.

That curiosity began early. Miller was born in 1935 in New Kensington, Pennsylvania, to a mother of Polish ancestry and a father whose family came from Germany. At age 15, his newspaper route carried him through the town’s different ethnic neighborhoods and helped spark his interest in journalism. He soon became a photographer for the local *Daily Dispatch*.

After high school, Miller served with the U.S. Army in Japan, Korea, and China. Rather than combat duty, he worked as a military photographer, documenting events with still and motion-picture cameras.

Returning home, he enrolled at Kent State University and became the first member of his family to earn a college degree. There he met Marianne Spaethling, a young German woman who shared his energy, curiosity, and enthusiasm for people. They married and later moved to Chicago, where Miller earned a master’s degree from Northwestern University’s journalism program.

When several major newspapers offered him jobs, Miller chose *The Plain Dealer*. He started on Labor Day 1961 and remained at the newspaper for 40 years.

His assignments eventually took him far beyond Cleveland. Miller reported internationally and was nominated for a Pulitzer Prize for his coverage of the fall of communism in Europe. His career earned nearly 100 journalism and civic honors, including high national decorations from Germany and Poland and induction into the Cleveland Journalism Hall of Fame.

Yet Cleveland’s ethnic communities remained closest to his heart. Even after retiring in 2001, Miller continued attending the festivals, cultural programs, and gatherings of the people he had written about. He never stopped asking questions or learning from the city around him.

His impact also reached Cleveland’s physical landscape. Miller was an important advocate in the effort to preserve and restore Playhouse Square at a time when its historic theaters faced an uncertain future. His name remains on a plaque inside the Palace Theatre alongside others who helped turn preservation into one of Cleveland’s major cultural success stories.

A stroke in 2009 took away the booming voice so many Clevelanders remembered, but not the body of work he left behind.

William Miller’s Cleveland legacy is the city he recorded in all its complexity. He helped generations of readers see that Polish, Slovenian, Hungarian, Irish, German, Arab, Asian, African, Latino, and countless other histories were not separate from Cleveland’s story—they were the story.

Basil M. Russo has spent decades building institutions that connect Cleveland’s Italian American heritage with law, education, philanthropy, public culture, and national civic life.

A native Clevelander, Russo built his early career in law and public service. He served on Cleveland City Council and became Majority Leader, later serving as a judge on the Cuyahoga County Court of Common Pleas and the Ohio Court of Appeals. He also founded Russo, Rosalina & Co., where he practiced until retiring in 2014. His judicial service earned recognition from the Ohio Supreme Court.

Russo’s Italian American work has been equally rooted in Cleveland institutions. He has served as President of the Justinian Forum, bringing together Italian American lawyers and judges in Greater Cleveland, and for years helped lead Cleveland’s Columbus Day Parade.

He also helped found the Cleveland Italian Film Festival and supported its role in raising funds for restoration of the Italian Cultural Garden in Rockefeller Park. Alongside other Italian American organizations, the festival helped direct substantial support toward preserving one of Cleveland’s historic Cultural Gardens.

In 1995, Russo helped establish the Bishop Anthony Pilla Italian American Studies Program at John Carroll University. The program created a permanent academic setting for examining Italian and Italian American history, culture, immigration, and identity.

He was also a founding trustee of the Northeast Ohio Italian American Foundation, which has directed millions of dollars toward charitable and cultural causes.

Russo carried that Cleveland experience onto a national stage. In 2014, he became National President of Italian Sons and Daughters of America and its affiliated financial organization. Under his tenure, ISDA expanded its digital reach and national programming; as of 2026, its leadership biography reports more than 730,000 social-media followers and more than $474 million in financial assets.

He later became President of the Conference of Presidents of Major Italian American Organizations, a coalition now representing 77 cultural, educational, charitable, fraternal, and advocacy organizations. He previously served on the National Italian American Foundation’s board and executive committee.

His family has also connected Cleveland with contemporary film culture. Russo served as executive producer of *Pieces*, written and directed by his sons Anthony and Joseph Russo. The family later helped establish a filmmaker program providing grants to emerging artists exploring Italian American stories.

Russo and his wife, Patricia, also served Cleveland’s Catholic community through advisory work in marriage and family ministry. Together they raised four children—Gabriella, Angela, Anthony, and Joseph—and their family’s professional lives have remained connected to law, education, media, and film.

Basil Russo’s Cleveland legacy is the network of institutions he helped strengthen: an Italian Cultural Garden, film festival, university studies program, legal association, charitable foundation, and cultural organizations that connect local heritage with national and international Italian American life. His career shows how Cleveland’s ethnic institutions can preserve their history while building new educational, civic, and cultural opportunities.

Sister Alicia Alvarado spent her life helping Cleveland’s Latino families find a stronger voice within the institutions around them. Her work moved between neighborhood organizations, the Catholic Church, social services, higher education, and City Hall—often connecting people who needed assistance with systems that had not always been easy to navigate.

Born in Villalba, Puerto Rico, in 1948, Alvarado came to Cleveland at age six with her family. She grew up on the city’s West Side, attending public school as well as St. Wendelin, St. Patrick, and St. Stephen schools.

Education became one of the foundations of her work. Alvarado studied at Cuyahoga Community College, earned a degree in Spanish and Secondary Education from Cleveland State University, pursued graduate social-work study at Case Western Reserve University, and later studied journalism and broadcast communications at Kent State University.

Before entering religious life, she worked as Social Services Coordinator for Cleveland’s Spanish American Committee, giving her direct experience with the practical challenges facing Latino families. In 1979, she entered the Sisters of St. Dominic of Akron, later part of the Dominican Sisters of Peace, and made her final profession in 1985.

Her religious vocation remained firmly connected to Cleveland’s Hispanic community. From 1982 to 1984, she served as Hispanic Program Coordinator for the Cleveland Diocese’s Commission on Catholic Community Action. She later worked in Hispanic ministry in Toledo and spent six years in St. Louis, including leadership of the Catholic Hispanic Center and Los Caminantes Project. In 1998, she returned to Northeast Ohio as Director of the Cleveland Diocese’s Hispanic Office.

Alvarado’s work regularly crossed the boundary between church ministry and civic life. She became the first Hispanic woman appointed to the Cuyahoga Community College Board of Trustees in 2001, bringing Latino representation into one of Northeast Ohio’s largest educational institutions.

She later served as Executive Assistant to Cleveland Ward 14 Councilman Joe Santiago. The position placed a longtime neighborhood organizer inside city government, where she could connect residents, churches, organizations, and public officials around concerns affecting one of Cleveland’s most heavily Latino neighborhoods.

Her leadership reached beyond the city as well. Alvarado represented Ohio within the Midwest Catholic Association of Hispanic Ministry and served in leadership positions within the organization. She also served on the National Farm Worker Ministry Board and traveled to Colombia, Chile, El Salvador, and Nicaragua as part of her work for social justice.

In 2005, her fellow Dominican sisters elected her to a four-year leadership term within her congregation. Whether serving within the Church, a college boardroom, City Hall, or a neighborhood organization, Alvarado repeatedly brought the concerns of people with limited institutional power into places where decisions were made.

Her work earned the Individual Award for Justice and Peace from the Cleveland Commission on Catholic Community Action, the Hispanic Business Association’s Community Relations Award, the Madrina—or “Godmother of the Community”—Award, and the Cleveland Hispanic Roundtable’s Lifetime Community Service Award.

Sister Alicia Alvarado died in 2022 at age 73. Her Cleveland legacy is the network of connections she spent decades strengthening: Latino families to social services, immigrant communities to the Church, students to higher education, neighborhoods to City Hall, and local struggles to broader movements for social justice. She helped make Cleveland institutions more accessible while ensuring that Latino residents were increasingly present within the institutions themselves.

Sheila Murphy Crawford has spent much of her life making Irish culture something Clevelanders can dance, hear, visit, celebrate, and pass to another generation.

Born and raised in Cleveland, Crawford grew up in an Irish American family rooted in Counties Cork and Westmeath. Her parents, Ollie and Betty Murphy, emphasized service to others and were themselves active in Cleveland’s Irish cultural life. Crawford attended Christ the King School and Regina High School before earning a degree in education from the University of Dayton and a master’s degree in English from Cleveland State University.

She taught English at Brush High School for 32 years, while also spending 20 years coaching the majorette corps, coaching athletic teams, and choreographing school and community theater productions. She was named Teacher of the Year in 1973.

In 1978, after earning certification in Ireland as both an Irish dance teacher and adjudicator, Crawford founded the Murphy Irish Arts Center. She later established the nonprofit Murphy Irish Arts Association to support Irish cultural education and programming.

The Murphy Irish Dancers became a familiar presence throughout Cleveland, performing at festivals, civic events, and St. Patrick’s Day celebrations. Crawford led the dancers in 39 consecutive Cleveland St. Patrick’s Day Parades, while students trained under her competed throughout North America and abroad. In 2015, the senior Dance Drama Team won a first-place World Championship title in Montreal.

Crawford’s involvement in Irish dance stretches across Cleveland history. She has participated in every Cleveland Feis since its founding in 1957—first as a competitor and later as a teacher and adjudicator. In 2015, the North American Feis Commission inducted her into its Hall of Fame for lifetime service to Irish dance.

Her leadership also reached many of Cleveland’s Irish organizations. Crawford served five terms as President of the Ladies Ancient Order of Hibernians and, with her sister Joan, spent ten years co-directing the Ohio Degree Team. She has taught ceili dancing through the Cleveland Gaelic Society and Irish American Club East Side and has been active with the West Side Irish American Club and United Irish Societies, where her service dates to the 1970s.

Her deepest public legacy may be in the Cleveland Cultural Gardens. Following in the footsteps of her parents, Crawford became Director of the Irish Cultural Garden in 1993 and helped lead a major restoration of the site. Over more than four decades in the Gardens, she served eight years as Vice President of the Cleveland Cultural Gardens Federation, five years as Chair of its Design and Preservation Committee, and five years as Federation President.

That leadership extended well beyond the Irish Garden. Crawford chaired One World Day during a period when the celebration drew roughly 20,000 visitors and helped lead the Cultural Gardens’ 100th anniversary observances in 2016. Her work helped strengthen the idea that preserving one community’s heritage could also bring Cleveland’s many communities together.

Her service has been recognized repeatedly. She was named Hibernian of the Year, received the Irish American Archives Society’s Walks of Life Award, was honored as an Irish Woman of Influence, and in 2018 became only the third woman in the history of Cleveland’s St. Patrick’s Day Parade to serve as Grand Marshal.

Crawford has always treated cultural education as more than performance. She taught generations of students to work hard, accept both victory and defeat with grace, serve others, and lead by doing the work themselves.

Sheila Murphy Crawford’s Cleveland legacy is visible across dance floors, parade routes, club halls, and Rockefeller Park. Through the Murphy Irish Arts Center, Irish Cultural Garden, Cleveland Feis, One World Day, and decades of teaching, she helped make Irish heritage a living part of the city rather than simply a memory of the past.

Dr. Atul C. Mehta has spent decades helping build Cleveland Clinic into an international center for advanced lung medicine. His Cleveland career combines clinical innovation, physician education, research, hospital leadership, and the creation of medical networks extending around the world.

Mehta became an early leader in interventional pulmonology, using advanced bronchoscopic techniques to diagnose and treat diseases of the lungs and airways. He helped establish and develop Cleveland Clinic programs in interventional pulmonology and lung transplantation and remains active in transplant, interventional, and general pulmonary medicine. Cleveland Clinic currently lists him as a Section Head within its lung-transplant team.

His influence has extended well beyond the patients he treated personally. Mehta trained, guided, or assisted more than 200 international medical professionals in establishing their careers. As Director of Cleveland Clinic’s Center for International Medical Education, he oversaw international physician applications, financial support, educational coordination, and programs bringing doctors from around the world to Cleveland for advanced training.

That network also worked in the opposite direction. Mehta became a link between international patients requiring highly specialized care and Cleveland Clinic’s transplant and tertiary-care services, helping bring patients and families from abroad into Cleveland’s medical system.

He strengthened Cleveland Clinic’s international presence through lectures, courses, and professional programs in more than 60 countries. His work included organizing medical symposia overseas, leading an early Cleveland Clinic management venture in India, and later taking on major medical leadership responsibilities at Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi.

At home, Mehta also built research and institutional capacity. He participated in pulmonary and transplant research, served in senior medical leadership, recruited and mentored physicians, and raised more than $3.7 million to support Cleveland Clinic programs. His teaching earned repeated recognition within the Clinic, and he became internationally recognized for contributions to bronchoscopy and interventional pulmonology. Cleveland Clinic notes that he helped found the American Association for Bronchology and played a formative role in the emerging field of interventional pulmonology.

One of the clearest examples of his impact on Cleveland came in 2012. Mehta helped secure and organize the 17th World Congress for Bronchology and Interventional Pulmonology, bringing nearly 900 specialists from 52 countries on six continents to the city. The gathering placed Cleveland Clinic physicians and Cleveland itself at the center of an international exchange of medical knowledge.

Dr. Atul Mehta’s Cleveland legacy is visible in a medical ecosystem that reaches far beyond one hospital: advanced pulmonary programs, generations of physicians he trained, international patients brought to Cleveland, research and education supported here, and specialists around the world who carried Cleveland-developed expertise back to their own institutions. His career helped make Cleveland not simply a place where complex lung disease is treated, but a place where the field itself has been taught and advanced.

Abdullah “Abby” Mina spent decades making Cleveland easier to navigate for Arab American immigrants while helping Lebanese and Middle Eastern culture become a more visible part of the city’s civic life.

Mina was born in Kefraya in Lebanon’s West Bekaa Valley, the seventh of eleven children of Michael and Labiba Mina. His early education included Islamic, Catholic, Protestant, and secular schools—an unusually diverse background that later informed his ability to work across religious and cultural communities.

He came to the United States for college and earned a B.A. in History and Political Science from the University of Richmond. There, he became active in student organizations, served as president of both the History Society and Philologian Literary Society, and was appointed editor-in-chief of the university’s literary magazine. Two cedar trees of Lebanon were later planted on campus in his honor.

Mina arrived in Cleveland in the mid-1960s and entered the insurance business. He later became a marketing consultant with Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Ohio, earning recognition for his sales achievements while building a parallel life of civic service.

His longest public commitment was to the Cleveland American Middle East Organization, or CAMEO. Mina became the organization’s longest-serving president and continued afterward as a member of its Board of Trustees. Through CAMEO, he helped connect Arab American residents with elected officials, civic institutions, and one another.

He also served as President of the Advisory Council of St. Elias Melkite Greek Catholic Church and worked with organizations including the International Services Center and Arab American social-service agencies, strengthening a network that supported immigrants as they established lives in Northeast Ohio.

For many Clevelanders, however, Mina was best known as the host and producer of a weekly Arabic-language radio program. The broadcast offered music and cultural programming but also served a practical purpose, sharing information that helped Arabic-speaking listeners understand immigration, government, and community resources.

Mina often provided that assistance personally. Over roughly 30 years, he helped complete or translate an estimated 1,000 immigration forms and official documents without accepting payment. He also interpreted in immigration courts in Cleveland and Cincinnati. In 1998, the Immigration and Naturalization Service formally recognized his assistance to immigrants, both individually and through his radio work.

His civic service extended into public institutions. In 2004, Mina was appointed foreman of a Cuyahoga County grand jury. In 2010, the U.S. Census Bureau honored him for outreach that encouraged participation among immigrant and ethnic populations, helping ensure those communities were counted and represented.

Mina also became an informal diplomatic and cultural connector. Among his memorable experiences were meeting King Hussein of Jordan and being invited to meet King Khaled of Saudi Arabia during the monarch’s visit to Cleveland.

His contributions earned numerous honors, including lifetime-achievement recognition from the Northern Ohio Lebanese American Association and the American Nationalities Movement’s Freedom Award for preserving Lebanese culture and promoting understanding among Cleveland’s many communities.

Mina built this public life alongside his wife, Mona, their two children, and three grandchildren. His personal interests in Arabic poetry, classical music, and Arabic music reflected the cultural traditions he spent decades sharing with others.

Abby Mina’s Cleveland legacy is unusually personal and practical. Through CAMEO, St. Elias, Arabic radio, immigration paperwork, courtroom interpretation, census outreach, and decades of unpaid assistance, he helped newcomers move from uncertainty toward participation—while giving Cleveland’s Arab American community a stronger and more enduring public voice.

Ralph J. “Rocky” Perk Jr. spent decades moving through many of Cleveland’s public institutions—as a neighborhood councilman, school-board president, attorney, municipal judge, and leader within the city’s nationality communities.

Born in Cleveland during World War II, Perk was the eldest son of Lucy Gagliardi Perk and future Mayor Ralph J. Perk. He attended Our Lady of Lourdes Grade School and High School, earned a B.S. in Business Administration from The Ohio State University in 1968, and was commissioned as an Army lieutenant through ROTC at John Carroll University. He was honorably discharged in 1976. In 1983, he earned his law degree from Cleveland-Marshall College of Law and passed the Ohio bar.

Perk entered public life while still a young man. Beginning in the late 1960s, he served five terms on Cleveland City Council representing neighborhoods largely associated today with Slavic Village. His committee work included Finance and Air Pollution, and his Council years included efforts to strengthen the city’s air-pollution regulations.

In the early 1980s, Perk moved from City Council into public education. He served on the Cleveland Board of Education and became its president in 1985 and again in 1989. Those years placed him in leadership during implementation of Cleveland’s federal school-desegregation order and during major labor negotiations affecting the district.

After completing his legal education, Perk entered the judiciary. He joined the Cleveland Municipal Court bench in 1991, retained his seat in that year’s election, and later won reelection. He served until retiring in January 2004. Afterward, he periodically returned to court as a visiting judge and served from 2008 to 2010 as a magistrate in Cuyahoga County Juvenile Court.

Perk’s public life has also remained deeply connected to Cleveland’s immigrant and ethnic organizations. In 2011, he became president of the American Nationalities Movement, succeeding longtime president Irene Morrow. His father had founded the organization in 1959 as a coalition of nationality groups concerned with cultural preservation and the political freedom of people living under authoritarian governments.

Under Perk, the organization continued its Captive Nations programs, Freedom Awards, and gatherings recognizing Clevelanders who preserve ethnic traditions or maintain connections to communities abroad. Records from its 2024 Captive Nations event still identify him as president.

His involvement crosses many of the communities represented in Cleveland’s international landscape. Perk has participated in organizations including CAMEO, Italian Sons and Daughters of America, the First Catholic Slovak Ladies Association, Czech Catholic Union, Sokol Greater Cleveland, and the Hungarian Business and Tradesmen’s Club. He has also remained active at Our Lady of Lourdes Parish and in legal, alumni, and scholarship organizations.

His service has received recognition from organizations associated with Slavic Village, Cleveland-Marshall College of Law, Mothers Against Drunk Driving, and the American Nationalities Movement.

Ralph Perk Jr.’s Cleveland legacy spans unusually different parts of city life. He represented Slavic Village in Council, helped govern Cleveland schools during a consequential period of desegregation, spent more than a decade on the municipal bench, and continued a family tradition of bringing Cleveland’s nationality groups into civic life. Together, those roles connect neighborhood government, education, law, and ethnic heritage across more than half a century of Cleveland history.

Dr. Akram Boutros led The MetroHealth System from 2013 to 2022 through one of the most consequential periods of change in the institution’s modern history. During his tenure, MetroHealth expanded healthcare throughout Cuyahoga County while beginning a complete rebuilding of its historic West 25th Street campus.

An internist with decades of hospital leadership experience, Boutros came to MetroHealth after a career managing academic, community, and specialty hospitals. He studied at St. John’s University and SUNY Downstate Medical Center and later completed Harvard Business School’s Advanced Management Program.

At MetroHealth, he pushed the public health system beyond the model of a single central hospital. New and expanded health centers, emergency departments, ExpressCare sites, pharmacies, and school-based programs brought care closer to where people lived. MetroHealth physicians began providing healthcare inside Cleveland schools, creating a direct link between the health system and students who might otherwise have difficulty reaching medical care.

At the same time, Boutros led an ambitious reconstruction of MetroHealth’s main campus. In 2017, the system entered the bond market on its own credit and sold approximately $946 million in hospital revenue bonds to finance its Campus Transformation. The project ultimately included a new hospital, expanded outpatient facilities, parking and infrastructure, and major changes to the West 25th Street campus.

Construction of the new 11-story hospital began in 2019. That building—the Glick Center—became the centerpiece of a broader redevelopment strategy intended not only to replace aging hospital facilities but also to improve the surrounding neighborhood and rethink how healthcare was delivered.

Boutros also helped move MetroHealth toward a broader definition of health. The system expanded initiatives addressing food, housing, education, addiction, violence, and other social and economic conditions that can determine whether people become sick in the first place. MetroHealth described this approach as extending its mission from patient care toward community health.

During his early years as CEO, MetroHealth added more than a thousand jobs, expanded clinical facilities, completed an $82 million Critical Care Pavilion addition, and reported substantial growth in both patient activity and operating revenue. The system simultaneously continued providing large amounts of free and uncompensated care as Cuyahoga County’s public safety-net hospital.

Boutros brought MetroHealth into Cleveland’s wider civic network as well. His service included organizations connected to the Greater Cleveland Partnership, Greater Cleveland Food Bank, United Way, Cuyahoga Community College, Cleveland Ballet, and national healthcare leadership. He also chaired the Cleveland Heart Ball and received regional recognition for healthcare and community leadership.

The original Hall of Fame biography captured only the first five years of this transformation. By the end of Boutros’s tenure, many of the projects planned during that period had moved from concept to construction, reshaping both MetroHealth and a major stretch of Cleveland’s West 25th Street corridor.

Dr. Akram Boutros’s Cleveland legacy is therefore unusually physical as well as institutional: healthcare sites distributed across the county, doctors working inside Cleveland schools, expanded critical-care facilities, and a rebuilt public-hospital campus. His tenure helped reposition MetroHealth as not only a place that treats illness, but a major civic institution capable of influencing health, employment, investment, and neighborhood development across Cleveland.

Ingrida Bublys has spent decades building practical connections between Cleveland, Ohio, and Lithuania through international trade, diplomacy, education, and culture.

She helped American companies enter markets in Lithuania and the Baltic region while assisting Lithuanian companies seeking customers, partners, and investment opportunities in the United States. Her work connected business leaders with government agencies and economic-development organizations in both countries.

Education became an important part of that diplomatic network. Bublys helped connect Ohio universities with institutions in Lithuania, creating opportunities for academic partnerships and exchanges. At the state level, she also helped establish cooperation between the Ohio Department of Agriculture and Lithuania’s Ministry of Agriculture.

Her work repeatedly brought Lithuania into Cleveland’s public life. She has organized visits by Lithuanian officials, supported cultural events, and helped visiting government representatives reach American civic and business leaders. In 2026, she remained an active presence at Cleveland events involving Lithuania’s ambassador and consul general.

Ingrida Bublys’s Cleveland legacy is the international network she made tangible: Lithuanian businesses entering American markets, Ohio companies reaching Europe, universities building partnerships, government agencies working together, and visiting diplomats finding a welcome and connections in Cleveland.
