Paul Burik has spent decades shaping both Cleveland’s built environment and the cultural landscape through which its immigrant communities tell their stories.

Born in České Budějovice—Budvar—in present-day Czechia, Burik fled Czechoslovakia with his father in 1968 after the Soviet-led invasion. That experience of leaving one country and rebuilding life in another later informed his commitment to preserving cultural identity within Cleveland.

Burik studied architecture at Kent State University and spent much of his professional career with the City of Cleveland, eventually serving as Chief Architect. His public work also included service on the Cleveland Landmarks Commission and Streetscape Committee, placing him directly in discussions about historic preservation, public architecture, streets, and neighborhood character. He retired from city service in 2010.

Architecture and cultural preservation came together most fully in his work with the Cleveland Cultural Gardens. Burik served as both President and Vice President of the Cleveland Cultural Gardens Federation, helping guide the organization that brings Cleveland’s many nationality gardens together within a shared public landscape.

His own Central European heritage has remained a major part of that work. Burik has served as President of the Cleveland chapter of the Czechoslovak Society of Arts and Sciences, promoting deeper understanding of Czech, Slovak, and Rusyn history and culture. He has also been active with Sokol Greater Cleveland, Cleveland-Bratislava Sister Cities, and the Carpatho-Rusyn Society.

Through these organizations, Burik helped connect Cleveland’s Czech and Slovak communities not only to their heritage but also to contemporary cultural exchange. His Sister City involvement linked Cleveland directly with Bratislava, while his work through SVU and Sokol supported lectures, cultural programs, and the preservation of traditions across generations.

His planning work extended beyond Cleveland to his home community of Avon. Burik co-founded the French Creek Foundation to strengthen and promote Avon’s historic downtown and later served as its president. As Chairman of the Avon Planning Commission, he helped develop the city’s master plan and zoning regulations, applying the same concern for place, history, and thoughtful development that shaped his Cleveland work.

Burik has also spent years introducing young people to sailing through the Lorain Sailing and Yacht Club. He served the organization as rear commodore, vice commodore, and commodore while volunteering as a sailing instructor.

Together with his wife, Fran, Burik has a combined family of five adult children and eight grandchildren.

Paul Burik’s Cleveland legacy joins two kinds of preservation: preserving the physical character of a city and preserving the histories of the people who built it. Through architecture, landmarks, streetscapes, the Cultural Gardens, and Central European organizations, he helped ensure that Cleveland’s public spaces carry both civic function and cultural memory.

Richard J. Fleischman helped define modern architecture in Cleveland through a career spanning nearly six decades and hundreds of buildings, public plans, interiors, and works of design.

Born in Cleveland in 1928, Fleischman showed an early fascination with drawing and building models. An uncle recognized that interest and encouraged him to pursue architecture. At East Technical High School, Fleischman earned a scholarship to Carnegie Institute of Technology, now Carnegie Mellon University, where he completed its five-year architecture program.

He continued at Columbia University, earning a master’s degree in architecture. A traveling fellowship then allowed him to study major buildings and public spaces in Italy, Spain, Greece, Germany, and Scandinavia. Those experiences helped form his lifelong belief that architecture was fundamentally about shaping space—an idea he described as both “sculpted space” and the “beauty of emptiness.”

Fleischman returned to Cleveland and worked with architect William Conrad before the two formed Conrad and Fleischman Architects in 1961. He went on to lead his own firm for 57 years. By the end of his career, he had completed nearly 500 projects and received roughly 280 design and professional awards.

His architecture became recognizable for clean geometric forms, large expanses of glass, natural light, and open interiors. He designed schools, university buildings, offices, libraries, performing-arts spaces, and civic structures throughout Ohio, but religious architecture became one of his particular specialties. His churches—including St. Paschal Baylon in Highland Heights—helped earn him a reputation as a master church designer.

Fleischman’s Cleveland impact reached beyond individual buildings. He participated in the early master planning for the Gateway complex, helping shape ideas behind the redevelopment that brought new sports facilities and investment into downtown Cleveland.

He also imagined possibilities for Cleveland that were never fully built. His “Ohio Riviera” proposal envisioned the Lake Erie shoreline as a continuous urban waterfront combining public access with places to live, work, learn, and gather. The concept reflected his belief that architecture and city planning should shape the experience of an entire community, not simply individual structures.

His design work crossed disciplinary boundaries. Fleischman created furniture for Italian manufacturer Saporiti and designed *The Dancers*, an abstract metal sculpture for the Putnam Collection at Case Western Reserve University.

His professional peers repeatedly recognized his influence. Fleischman was elected a Fellow of the American Institute of Architects in 1974. His Cleveland firm received AIA Ohio’s Gold Medal in 1988, and Fleischman himself received the organization’s individual Gold Medal in 2001. He was also awarded the Cleveland Arts Prize for design in 1974.

Even late in life, Fleischman continued advising clients, students, and younger architects, treating architecture as an ongoing conversation about beauty, proportion, light, and public space.

Richard Fleischman died in 2020 at age 91. His Cleveland legacy remains visible not only in individual buildings, but in a broader way of thinking about the city: architecture as the art of creating spaces people share, and Cleveland itself as a place whose streets, institutions, lakefront, and public buildings could be designed with imagination.

Marilyn Madigan has spent a lifetime serving Cleveland through healthcare, parish leadership, and Irish American cultural organizations. A lifelong West Park resident, many of her most important contributions grew from the same neighborhood institutions that shaped her as a child.

The daughter of Jack and Catherine Finn Madigan, with family roots in Ireland, Madigan attended St. Patrick West Park Grade School and St. Joseph Academy. At St. Patrick, she participated in and later coached Catholic Youth Organization activities, beginning a connection to the parish that would become one of the defining commitments of her life.

When St. Patrick West Park was ordered closed, Madigan became a leader in the parishioners’ canonical appeal to the Vatican’s Congregation for the Clergy. The appeal succeeded, and the parish reopened after two years. Madigan then served as Parish Council President, Eucharistic Minister, and collection counter, helping rebuild parish life after the closure.

Her professional career was equally rooted in service. Madigan earned a B.S. in Nursing from St. John College and began at Rainbow Babies & Children’s Hospital in pediatric intensive care. She later became an Advanced Clinical Nurse in Operative Services at University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center, where she spent 38 years. She retired in 2018 after a 41-year nursing career at University Hospitals.

Madigan’s involvement with Cleveland’s Irish community began in 1969, when she marched in the St. Patrick’s Day Parade with the West Side Irish American Club’s Ladies Drill Team. She also played the Irish sport of camogie, became president of the Emerald Camogie Team, and served as Registrar of the North American Camogie Board.

Over the decades, her Irish cultural involvement expanded across the region. She has been associated with Cleveland Comhaltas, the Gaelic Society, Irish American Club East Side, Irish Northern Aid, United Irish Societies, West Side Irish American Club, Cleveland Feis, Irish Music Academy of Cleveland, Cleveland Irish Cultural Festival, Ohio Irish Festival, and Irish American Archives Society. She also studied Irish dance with the O’Leary Manning School.

Madigan took leadership roles rather than simply attending events. She served as a board member and vice president of the Irish Music Academy, trustee of the West Side Irish American Club, co-chair of the Ohio Irish Festival, deputy director of the United Irish Societies, and treasurer of Cleveland Comhaltas.

Her most sustained national leadership came through the Ladies Ancient Order of Hibernians. During more than 40 years of membership, Madigan served as Division, County, and State President and helped found the Ohio State Degree Team. Nationally, she served as Fundraiser from 2012 to 2014, Irish Historian from 2014 to 2016, Treasurer from 2016 to 2018, and later National Secretary.

Marilyn Madigan’s Cleveland legacy connects three forms of service that defined her life: caring for patients, protecting a neighborhood parish, and sustaining Irish culture. From University Hospitals and St. Patrick West Park to Cleveland’s parade, clubs, music, dance, and Hibernian organizations, she helped keep institutions alive by doing the everyday work required for them to endure.

Sree N. Sreenath has spent decades using Cleveland as a base for work that connects engineering, global development, education, and community service.

His research included systems-biology applications involving leukemia, prostate cancer, and hydrocephalus, alongside work on global issues such as energy, water, climate, and sustainable development.

He also built programs that connected Case Western Reserve to institutions around the world. From 1996 to 2006, Sreenath co-directed the UNESCO GENIe Program, an international educational network. From 2007 to 2016, he directed Case’s Complex Systems Biology Center, and he also led the university’s Graduate Engineering & Management National and International program. He continues at Case as a professor and currently serves as Program Director for the Master of Engineering program.

Sreenath’s scholarship regularly moved outside the university. He published technical work on global warming as early as 1990 and participated in international work involving climate, water, and development policy. His professional service included global water initiatives as well as committees associated with major U.S. science and health agencies. He lectured in 25 countries and organized more than 40 workshops, conferences, and symposia.

His teaching also earned recognition, including Case awards for undergraduate instruction. Across his academic work, Sreenath repeatedly linked technical education to problems that cross national and disciplinary boundaries.

That same approach shaped his civic life in Northeast Ohio. He served organizations including the Federation of India Community Associations, Kasturi Kannada Association, and Sri Venkateswara Temple, helping sustain cultural, educational, and service institutions within Greater Cleveland’s Indian American community.

His largest service role came through Sewa International USA. Sreenath served as national president from 2009 to 2020, helping strengthen and expand an organization devoted to disaster recovery, education, family services, and development. Sewa today operates a national network of more than 40 chapters and lists Sreenath among its former presidents and advisors.

Cleveland became one of those active service centers. The local Sewa chapter operates education programs such as ASPIRE, along with family services, community development, and volunteer initiatives. Sree Sreenath’s Cleveland legacy lies in connecting worlds that are often kept separate: engineering and social problems, university research and public service, Indian cultural traditions and American education, and local volunteering with international development. Jeanette Grasselli Brown spent her career moving between the laboratory, the boardroom, the university, and Cleveland’s civic institutions—using scientific expertise as a foundation for leadership in education, culture, healthcare, and public service.

Brown earned a B.S. from Ohio University and an M.S. in Chemistry from Case Western Reserve University. She then spent 38 years in industrial research with The Standard Oil Company, later BP America, ultimately becoming Director of Corporate Research.

Her specialty was vibrational spectroscopy, particularly infrared and Raman techniques used to identify materials and solve industrial problems. Her work extended into computerized spectroscopy, process analysis and control, environmental spectroscopy, and other advanced analytical methods. Over her career, she authored or co-authored more than 80 publications and nine books and held a patent.

Brown became an international leader in analytical chemistry. She served as national president of the Society for Applied Spectroscopy, chaired the Analytical Division of the American Chemical Society, and chaired the U.S. National Committee for the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry. From 1989 to 1995, she edited the international journal *Vibrational Spectroscopy*. She was also elected a Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science.

Her influence extended into corporate governance as well, with service on the boards of six Fortune 500 companies. She also participated in a White House advisory effort examining scientific and technological cooperation between the United States and Japan.

After retiring from BP in 1989, Brown turned increasingly toward higher education. At Ohio University, she served as Distinguished Visiting Professor and Director of Research Enhancement. In 1995, Governor George Voinovich appointed her to the Ohio Board of Regents, and Governor Bob Taft later reappointed her. She eventually chaired the board, helping guide statewide higher-education policy. In 2002, she also served as Vice Chair of the Governor’s Commission on Teacher Success.

Her Cleveland civic work was equally broad. Brown served or led efforts involving the Cleveland Clinic Foundation, Cleveland Orchestra, Great Lakes Science Center, Holden Arboretum, ideastream, Cleveland Scholarship Programs, and the Northeastern Ohio Science and Engineering Fair.

She took particular interest in young scientists. In 2003, Brown co-chaired the Intel International Science and Engineering Fair when Cleveland hosted students and researchers from around the world, giving the city a major role in one of the largest international showcases for student science.

Brown also remained active in Cleveland’s Hungarian American community through the Cleveland Hungarian Development Panel and related civic work. Her contributions to Hungarian American life helped earn her the Ellis Island Medal of Honor in 2002.

Her scientific and civic achievements brought numerous honors. Other recognition included the Great American Award from the Stan Hywet Foundation and Cleveland State University’s In Tribute to Public Service Award.

Jeanette Grasselli Brown’s Cleveland legacy lies in the way she carried scientific leadership into public institutions. She helped strengthen Cleveland’s research culture, supported young scientists, guided higher education, served major cultural and medical organizations, and remained active in Hungarian American civic life. Her career demonstrated that scientific achievement could become a form of civic leadership.

Dr. Dieu Thuc Do helped build some of the civic, religious, and cultural foundations of Vietnamese American life in Cleveland while establishing a long career as a physician.

Born in Rach Gia, Vietnam, Do was the oldest of five children. His father served as Deputy Chief of Rach Gia, and public service became part of Do’s own life early. After graduating from Saigon Medical School in 1965, he served as a physician and major in the Army of the Republic of Vietnam. From 1973 until the fall of South Vietnam in 1975, he also served as the elected chairman of the Rach Gia City Council.

After immigrating to the United States in 1975, Do had to rebuild a professional career he had already established in Vietnam. He completed the required medical equivalency examinations and residency training before returning to practice. He and his wife, Thuy, settled in Cleveland, where they raised their children, Francis, Stephanie, and Jennifer.

Beginning in 1980, Do practiced medicine in Cleveland. Patients came to know him for an approach that considered not only illness, but also family circumstances, cultural background, personal values, and individual choice. For many, the relationship extended beyond the examining room, making him a trusted presence within the families he served.

The same year he began practicing in Cleveland, Do became President of the Vietnamese Community in Greater Cleveland. From 1980 to 1988, he helped a newly established refugee and immigrant population create organizations, maintain traditions, and navigate unfamiliar public systems. He frequently served as a bridge between Vietnamese families and Cleveland government.

That role expanded citywide when Do joined the Cleveland Mayor’s Advisory Committee, serving from 1983 to 1993. He also co-founded the Asian Pacific American Federation, helping Vietnamese concerns become part of a broader Asian American civic presence in Northeast Ohio.

Faith provided another base for institution-building. A practicing Catholic, Do worked with the Vietnamese Catholic Community at St. Boniface, the Diocese of Cleveland’s Asian Ministry, and diocesan vocational programs. He also served on the Board of Trustees of Cleveland Catholic Charities, connecting immigrant experience with one of the region’s major social-service networks.

Do’s military service also continued in his adopted country. He joined the U.S. Army Reserve and served during Operation Desert Storm in 1991, later retiring as a major. In Cleveland, he remained active in observances honoring both American and Vietnamese veterans, including Veterans Day and annual April 30 commemorations marking the fall of Saigon.

Do and his family also participated in cultural programs such as the Lorain International Festival and the Diocese of Cleveland’s Church in the City initiative. For one of Cleveland’s earliest generations of Vietnamese immigrants, these events offered a way to preserve language, history, faith, and tradition while sharing them with neighbors from other communities.

Dr. Dieu Thuc Do’s Cleveland legacy is visible in the institutions a new immigrant community needed in order to take root: medical care, cultural organizations, church networks, relationships with City Hall, and public remembrance. By rebuilding his own life after displacement and then helping others do the same, he became part of the first generation that transformed Vietnamese presence in Cleveland into an enduring civic community.

Robert “Bob” Haas has spent decades creating ways for people in Greater Cleveland to know their neighbors—first through public safety and neighborhood organizing, and later through one of the region’s largest cultural festivals.

Born and raised on Cleveland’s West Side, Haas graduated from St. Edward High School, attended John Carroll University, and completed training at the Ohio Highway Patrol Police Academy. He then began a 35-year career with the Berea Police Department, serving as a patrol officer, detective, and eventually Community Relations Officer before retiring in 2010.

Community-building became a central part of his police work. Haas founded Berea’s Block Watch program, helping residents organize around neighborhood safety, and played an important role in establishing Safety Town, where generations of children and families learned practical lessons about traffic and personal safety.

His interest in cultural life grew from his own family. Haas’s grandparents immigrated from Germany, and his parents kept German food, music, holidays, and customs alive at home. Among his strongest childhood memories were family trips to Kiefer’s Restaurant at Detroit Avenue and West 25th Street, once a familiar gathering place for Cleveland’s German American community.

While working in Berea, Haas also became familiar with Oktoberfest celebrations held at the Cuyahoga County Fairgrounds. When the festival moved away and eventually disappeared, he became determined to restore a tradition that had once brought thousands of people together.

In 2005, Haas worked with volunteers from Berea Kiwanis, Berea Rotary, the Donauschwaben community, and other local organizations to revive the event as the Cleveland Oktoberfest. As founder and executive director, he helped develop it into a major Northeast Ohio celebration of German heritage through traditional music, dance, food, and public festivities.

His service on the board of the Cuyahoga County Fairgrounds helped strengthen the festival’s long-term home in Berea and its relationship with the surrounding community.

Haas soon saw an opportunity to make the festival serve an even larger purpose. Many smaller ethnic festivals across Greater Cleveland were struggling with rising costs and declining attendance. In response, he founded the William F. Miller International Pavilion, creating a shared venue where cultural organizations could perform before the much larger Oktoberfest audience.

The Pavilion has featured music, dance, clothing, and traditions from more than 20 ethnic communities. Rather than treating cultures as isolated celebrations, Haas created a place where audiences could move from one tradition to another in a single setting.

That idea reflects his broader view of Cleveland. Communities may speak different languages, prepare different foods, or trace their histories to different parts of the world, but they also gather around many of the same things: family, music, dancing, celebration, and friendship.

Bob Haas’s Cleveland legacy connects two careers that at first seem very different. Whether organizing Block Watch groups, teaching children through Safety Town, reviving Oktoberfest, or opening a stage to dozens of cultural communities, his work has consistently been about community relations—creating circumstances in which people meet, participate, and discover something about one another.

Helen Karpinski spent more than half a century opening doors for women in Cleveland public life while strengthening the Polish American organizations and cultural institutions that shaped her own community.

Born in Cleveland in 1899, Karpinski grew up in a large Polish American family and spent part of her childhood in Reynoldsville, Pennsylvania. She left school after eighth grade to work, then returned to Cleveland as a teenager in search of greater opportunity.

She married Johnny Karpinski, a noted amateur boxer and political organizer in Cleveland’s Polish community. After his death, Helen succeeded him as a precinct committeeperson and developed a political career that would eventually reach from neighborhood wards to national party leadership.

From the late 1930s into 1950, Karpinski served as a Cleveland Democratic ward leader. In 1939, she made city political history by becoming the first woman under Cleveland’s current charter to survive a City Council primary, finishing ahead of an incumbent. She lost the general election, but later women candidates remembered the race as proof that a woman could challenge the established political structure.

Karpinski spent the rest of her life helping other women enter public life. As president of the Federated Democratic Women of Ohio, she helped recruit Gertrude Donahey for state treasurer and organized women across the state to campaign for her. Karpinski chaired Donahey’s successful 1970 campaign, which made Donahey the first woman elected to a statewide administrative office in Ohio.

Her own service reached well beyond party politics. Karpinski worked as Deputy Clerk of the Cuyahoga County Jury Commission, served on the Cleveland Civil Service Commission, and later sat on the Cuyahoga Board of Tax Revision. She also served at county and state party levels and, from 1980 to 1984, on the Democratic National Committee and its Ethnic Committee.

Polish civic life remained equally important. Karpinski served as president of the American Polish Women’s Club, spent more than 20 years as an officer in the Polish Women’s Alliance of America, and participated in the Alliance of Poles, Polish Congress–Ohio Division, and Polish veterans’ organizations. She also founded the Ave Maria Senior Citizens Club at St. Casimir Church.

Her longest cultural commitment was to the Cleveland Cultural Gardens. Beginning in 1945, Karpinski helped establish and represent the Polish Cultural Garden and served the Federation as treasurer, financial secretary, vice president, and trustee of its endowment fund. Her involvement continued for decades.

Karpinski also helped lead the campaign to place a bronze bust of scientist Marie Skłodowska Curie in the Polish Garden. Polish American women raised the money over years through community events and small fundraisers, turning their collective effort into a permanent monument within Cleveland’s public landscape.

Her work in the Gardens reinforced a larger belief that ethnic identity could become a basis for cooperation rather than separation. She helped found and lead the Women’s Cosmopolitan Democratic League, bringing women from different communities together around civic participation and mutual understanding.

Karpinski’s influence extended into her own family. Her three daughters all became attorneys and continued traditions of civic and public service.

Helen Karpinski died in 2002 at age 102. Her Cleveland legacy joins several histories that are often told separately: women entering political power, Polish immigrants building civic institutions, and nationality groups creating a shared public culture. Through campaigns, government service, women’s organizations, and the Cultural Gardens, she helped make Cleveland’s civic life more representative of the people who lived here.

Alex Machaskee spent more than four decades at *The Plain Dealer* while becoming one of the civic leaders who connected Cleveland’s journalism, arts, philanthropy, business, and international communities.

Born in Warren, Ohio, Machaskee began as a sports and general-assignment reporter for the *Warren Tribune*. He later earned a bachelor’s degree in marketing from Cleveland State University and joined *The Plain Dealer* in 1960.

His career at the newspaper unfolded across nearly every side of its operations. Machaskee served as Promotion Director, Assistant to the Publisher, Director of Labor Relations and Personnel, and Vice President and General Manager before being named Publisher in 1990. As Publisher, President, and CEO, he was responsible for the overall policy, operation, and direction of Ohio’s largest newspaper until his retirement in 2006.

That role placed Machaskee at the center of Cleveland public life during decades of economic change, neighborhood transformation, civic redevelopment, and growing international connections. His influence extended well beyond the pages of the newspaper.

Machaskee served in leadership roles with some of Cleveland’s most important cultural institutions, including the Cleveland Orchestra, Cleveland Museum of Art, and University Circle Inc. A musician himself, he remained a strong advocate for the performing arts and for the institutions that made Cleveland a major cultural center.

His civic service also included the Cleveland Council on World Affairs, Crime Stoppers of Cuyahoga County, and United Way Services. He chaired a United Way campaign and later became a Lifetime Director, linking business leadership with organizations addressing health, education, family, and social-service needs throughout Greater Cleveland.

International affairs became another defining part of his work. As Chairman of International Orthodox Christian Charities, Machaskee traveled through Europe, the Middle East, and Africa to oversee humanitarian relief efforts firsthand. That work joined Cleveland-based leadership with international responses to poverty, conflict, and displacement.

He also served as Honorary Consul of the Republic of Serbia and participated in Cleveland’s Foreign Consular Corps. Through these roles, Machaskee helped connect Northeast Ohio’s ethnic communities, civic institutions, and business leaders with governments and organizations abroad.

Education remained another important part of his Cleveland ties. Cleveland State University awarded him an honorary Doctor of Humane Letters in 1995, and he later received honorary degrees from the University of Akron and Heidelberg College.

His journalism, humanitarian, and civic work earned recognition including the Urban League of Cleveland’s Whitney M. Young Humanitarian Award, World Trade Center Cleveland’s International Executive of the Year Award, the International Services Center’s Golden Door Award, and the Ellis Island Medal of Honor. Alex Machaskee’s Cleveland legacy lies in the unusually broad network of institutions he helped strengthen. From *The Plain Dealer* and United Way to the Cleveland Orchestra, Museum of Art, World Affairs community, and international humanitarian organizations, his career helped connect the city’s public conversation with its cultural life and with the wider world.

Lonnie Davis McCauley devoted her life to making Cleveland’s Irish American history something future generations could find, read, hear, perform, and remember.

Born in Cleveland on September 19, 1947, McCauley attended Lourdes Academy and earned a B.A. in Sociology from Cleveland State University. Years later, she returned to school and earned a master’s degree in library science from Kent State University in 1999. As part of that work, she interned at Trinity College in Dublin, fulfilling a lifelong dream, and wrote *The Irish Directory of Greater Cleveland*, documenting the organizations and resources that made up the region’s Irish cultural life.

Her involvement with Cleveland’s Irish organizations began formally in 1981 as Public Relations Secretary for the Irish-American Club East Side. Four years later, she helped found the Padraic Pearse Center and became its first president, serving seven terms.

Under McCauley’s leadership, the Center established Cleveland’s first Irish American library, giving books, records, and cultural materials a permanent home. She later helped create a second Irish American library at the West Side Irish-American Club, extending that effort across the city.

McCauley believed culture had to be practiced as well as preserved. She created *Voices of Ireland*, a seven-year program bringing together poetry, music, song, dance, recitation, and drama. She helped introduce Irish-language classes, adult dance instruction, bodhrán lessons, and visiting speakers to Cleveland audiences.

She participated as fully as she organized. McCauley wrote and recited poetry, studied Irish dance, competed with the Irish Adult Dancers, and took part in the Cleveland Feis with her daughter Caitlin. She also served on the founding board of the Irish Music Academy of Cleveland.

Her commitment to preservation eventually became professional. McCauley became the first Irish American Archivist at the Western Reserve Historical Society and remained closely involved with the Irish American Archives Society. She understood archives not as collections of old papers, but as the evidence needed to keep earlier generations present in the city’s memory.

That belief also shaped her work on the Irish Famine Memorial. McCauley served on the committee that created the memorial in Cleveland’s Flats and, in September 2000, presided over the dedication of its 11-ton Celtic cross. The monument gave Cleveland a permanent place to remember those who died during the Great Famine and the millions whose emigration reshaped cities such as Cleveland.

In 2001, McCauley was selected as Grand Marshal of Cleveland’s St. Patrick’s Day Parade—the first woman to receive that honor in the parade’s 134-year history.

McCauley once warned that without deliberate preservation, the generations who built Cleveland’s Irish community could become “historical ghosts.” Her own work was an answer to that possibility.

Lonnie Davis McCauley died on March 18, 2001. Her Cleveland legacy remains in the libraries she founded, records she preserved, programs she created, memorial she helped build, and traditions she practiced herself. She helped ensure that Cleveland’s Irish past would remain not only remembered, but accessible to the people who came after it.

Irene Morrow built a Cleveland career that joined public administration with decades of leadership among the city’s Polish American and international communities.

Morrow spent 25 years in local government. For eight years, she served as Deputy Auditor of Cuyahoga County, overseeing payroll operations and helping modernize county record keeping through computerization. She then joined the City of Cleveland, where she spent 17 years as Personnel Administrator and Secretary of the Civil Service Commission.

At City Hall, Morrow helped administer employment testing for approximately 10,000 municipal workers across more than 800 job classifications. She also helped introduce computerized systems for testing and grading, bringing new technology into one of the basic systems through which Cleveland hired and promoted public employees.

After retiring from city government in 1989, Morrow remained active professionally, working in food management and service with golf courses, country clubs, and yacht clubs and later assisting the president of Elite Realty.

Her service earned recognition including the Polonia Foundation’s 1985 Polish Person of the Year award. She was also recognized by First Lady Barbara Bush as one of 40 outstanding women achievers in Ohio.

The American Nationalities Movement brought together representatives of Cleveland’s many immigrant and nationality communities, especially those with ties to countries living under communist or authoritarian governments. Morrow helped organize Captive Nations observances that gave Clevelanders a public forum to remember political repression abroad and advocate for the freedom of people whose families and homelands remained affected by it.

Her leadership was notable because it extended beyond her own Polish heritage. Morrow became known as an ally of many nationality groups, helping create common ground among communities with different languages, histories, and traditions. Her work earned recognition from organizations including the United Hungarian Societies and Cleveland’s Vietnamese community.

Through this network, Morrow helped make ethnic identity part of Cleveland’s civic life rather than something confined to individual clubs or neighborhoods. Polish, Hungarian, Vietnamese, and other groups could gather around shared concerns while also preserving their own histories and cultures.

Morrow built this public life alongside her husband, Edward. Together they raised six children and later welcomed six grandchildren.

Irene Morrow’s Cleveland legacy bridges two kinds of public service. Inside government, she helped modernize the systems that supported thousands of city and county employees. Outside it, she spent decades building relationships among Cleveland’s nationality communities and keeping questions of cultural memory, political freedom, and mutual understanding visible in the city’s public life.

Fr. Jim O’Donnell spent nearly half a century making Cleveland’s Central neighborhood the center of a ministry built on one simple idea: live with people, not at a distance from them.

Raised in East Cleveland, O’Donnell attended St. Philomena Grade School and Cathedral Latin High School before preparing for the priesthood at St. Jerome’s College in Ontario and St. Mary Seminary in Cleveland. He was ordained for the Diocese of Cleveland on May 19, 1956.

His early ministry included St. Colman Church in Cleveland, St. Mary Church in Avon, and eight years directing the Diocese’s Catholic Youth Organization. In 1974, he spent six weeks in Calcutta working with Mother Teresa in the Home for the Dying. The experience reinforced a conviction that ministry required physical closeness to people experiencing poverty and exclusion.

After further periods living and working among poor communities around the United States, O’Donnell returned to Cleveland. In 1977, he and Maggie Walsh-Conrad moved into the Central neighborhood around East 35th Street and began what became the Community of the Little Brothers and Sisters of the Eucharist. Their guiding idea was a “ministry of presence”—or, as O’Donnell described it, ministry **with** the poor rather than simply **to** the poor.

They lived where they served. Neighbors encountered them not only at church programs, but on the street, in homes, in gardens, and in the ordinary routines of neighborhood life. Relationships came first; programs followed.

One of the most visible results was housing. O’Donnell and Walsh-Conrad helped bring Habitat for Humanity into Central. Early construction efforts grew into a much larger redevelopment that contributed to more than 600 new homes in the neighborhood.

They also cultivated community gardens, working with neighbors and church partners to grow food for residents and local food programs. The work joined neighborhood renewal with something immediate: fresh food grown on the same blocks where they lived.

Their ministry eventually became a family as well. Walsh-Conrad became a licensed foster parent, and together they welcomed children from difficult circumstances into their home. Several remained permanently, giving O’Donnell a role he described not only as priest but as “Abba”—a spiritual father within the household they created.

O’Donnell’s work reached beyond Central. He ministered for years to women in prison, people in juvenile detention, people with disabilities and their families, and individuals struggling with addiction. He also became a spiritual director to priests and laypeople across the Diocese.

Even in later life at Ennis Court in Lakewood, O’Donnell continued hearing confessions, counseling residents, praying with them, and celebrating Mass when his health allowed. Retirement never fully separated him from the pattern of presence that had defined his ministry.

His Cleveland legacy is most tangible in Central: homes where vacant or deteriorated properties once stood, gardens growing between city blocks, families strengthened through foster care, and relationships built over decades. His contribution was not simply serving a neighborhood from outside it. He made the neighborhood his home and allowed its people to shape the work he did there.

Joseph P. Meissner spent decades using law as a practical tool for people and neighborhoods that often had little access to legal or political power. His Cleveland career connected civil rights, Legal Aid, environmental and utility advocacy, veterans service, refugee resettlement, and a remarkable long-term relationship with the Vietnamese community.

A graduate of St. Ignatius High School, Meissner attended Xavier University, graduating as valedictorian in 1963 with a degree in history and minors in mathematics and philosophy. He then earned his law degree from Harvard Law School in 1966.

At Harvard, Meissner became deeply involved in civil-rights work. He co-chaired the Harvard Civil Rights Committee, helped create and edit the *Harvard Civil Rights-Civil Liberties Law Review*, and worked in Alabama during the 1964 Freedom Summer. Before entering active military service, he returned to Cleveland, taught mathematics at Myron T. Herrick School, and performed legal work connected with the Congress of Racial Equality.

Military service took Meissner to Vietnam with the Army’s 5th Special Forces Group. Even there, his interests crossed military and cultural lines. During his free time he worked with the Vietnamese American Friendship Society, teaching English and discussing American civic institutions with Vietnamese young people. His service earned him a Bronze Star and two Army Commendation Medals.

After returning to Cleveland, Meissner joined the Legal Aid Society and began the work that would define much of his civilian career. From 1969 through 1975, he led neighborhood Legal Aid offices—first in Kinsman at East 79th Street and later on the West Side at Lorain and Fulton. He then became Director of Legal Aid’s Community Development Section, remaining associated with the organization for decades.

His practice treated neighborhoods themselves as clients. Meissner advised nearly 300 businesses and community organizations on incorporation, contracts, taxes, trademarks, utility regulation, environmental law, and other issues necessary to keep local institutions operating.

He also represented Cleveland residents in battles over basic household needs. Working with neighborhood and consumer organizations, Meissner participated in regulatory cases involving electric, gas, and telephone service. He and his clients helped establish Ohio’s Percentage of Income Payment Plan, which allowed qualifying households to connect utility payments to income, and supported fuel-assistance and telephone Lifeline programs intended to keep essential services available to low-income residents.

Environmental advocacy became another part of that neighborhood work. Meissner represented community organizations concerned about industrial air pollution and participated in legal and regulatory proceedings involving major Cleveland-area industrial facilities. Rather than separating environmental law from poverty law, his work treated clean air, affordable utilities, housing, and neighborhood stability as connected issues.

He was also a teacher within the profession. Through Legal Aid, Meissner helped mentor more than 200 students and beginning lawyers, introducing another generation to community-based legal practice.

His relationship with Cleveland’s Vietnamese community became one of the most distinctive parts of his life. In 1975, shortly after the fall of Saigon, Meissner co-chaired Vietnamese Information Services, an effort that helped newly arriving refugees navigate resettlement in the United States. Cleveland International Hall of Fame biographical records credit the program with assisting approximately 15,000 Vietnamese refugees.

That relationship continued for decades. As vice-director of the Friendship Foundation, founded by Gia-Hoa Ryan, Meissner participated in humanitarian, educational, legal, and professional exchanges with Vietnam, Cambodia, and other parts of Asia. He repeatedly returned to the region where he had once served as a soldier, this time accompanying lawyers, educators, medical workers, volunteers, and humanitarian projects.

His military service continued as well. Meissner remained in the Army Reserve, eventually reaching the rank of lieutenant colonel and serving as Deputy Commander of the 2nd Psychological Operations Group. In Cleveland, he stayed active with veterans organizations and served the Greater Cleveland Veterans Memorial organization, which helped maintain and improve the Veterans Memorial on Mall C downtown.

Meissner also wrote about both sides of his career. His books included *Legal Warriors*, reflecting on decades of community law and the people who fought for their rights, and *The Green Berets and Their Victories*, drawing from his continuing engagement with military history.

His work connected law to the everyday functioning of neighborhoods and transformed a relationship with Vietnam that began in war into decades of refugee assistance, cultural exchange, and humanitarian cooperation. Josef Holzer helped turn Cleveland’s Donauschwaben community from a network of immigrant families into an institution with a permanent home, youth programs, cultural organizations, and leaders prepared to carry its traditions forward.

He married Franziska Kufner, and in 1952 the couple immigrated to Cleveland with their young daughter, Ilse, and Holzer’s parents. He found work as an electrician with Ford Motor Company.

Like many newly arrived Donauschwaben families, the Holzers were rebuilding community as well as individual lives. When the Society of the Donauschwaben was founded in Cleveland in 1958, it offered immigrants a place to speak their language, maintain cultural traditions, form friendships, and recreate some of the communal life they had left behind.

Holzer quickly became one of its central organizers. He was elected president in 1966. Organizational records show him leading the Society of the Danube Swabians through 1982 and then serving as president of the Donauschwaben German-American Cultural Center from 1982 to 1997—approximately three decades of continuous presidential leadership. He also served the national Society of the Donauschwaben U.S.A. as a regional president.

His greatest tangible contribution was Lenau Park in Olmsted Township.

By 1970, the community had outgrown its earlier Banater Club. Members purchased property on Columbia Road and began developing a larger cultural campus. Holzer became a driving force behind a building effort that stretched across roughly 15 years, helping oversee planning, design, fundraising, construction, and the volunteer labor required to complete it. The main clubhouse was formally opened in May 1986.

The result was not simply a banquet hall. Lenau Park became a cultural home with spaces for meetings, dance practice, music, bowling, soccer, social gatherings, and community organizations. Programs in German language, folk dancing, brass music, sports, and other traditions gave children opportunities to experience their heritage directly rather than knowing it only through family stories.

Holzer understood that a cultural institution could survive only if younger people eventually became responsible for it. He continually encouraged children and young adults to participate, volunteer, and move into leadership. He affectionately called the club’s children “our future”; many knew him simply as “Uncle Sepp.”

That emphasis on succession may have been as important as any building he helped construct. Holzer did not treat heritage as something the founding immigrant generation owned. He treated it as something they were responsible for teaching others how to maintain.

When the Lenau Park clubhouse opened in 1986, Holzer did not consider the work finished. He remained president for another decade, supporting programs, improving the property, and helping secure the organization’s financial future. After stepping down, he became Honorary President and Director of Operations.

Even in his eighties, Holzer remained a familiar presence at Lenau Park—dealing with maintenance and operations, welcoming people in the restaurant, visiting with longtime members, and forming relationships with younger ones. His leadership depended as much on everyday presence and trust as it did on formal titles.

Holzer died on April 8, 2013, at age 86, one month before he was scheduled to enter the Cleveland International Hall of Fame. His May 8 induction became a memorial celebration, with Donauschwaben president Margot Maurer inducting him, his daughter Ilse Jung representing the family, and grandson David Jung accepting the honor.

Josef Holzer’s Cleveland legacy can still be located on the map. Lenau Park gave generations of Donauschwaben families a place to gather, dance, play music, learn German, play sports, celebrate, and teach children where their families came from. But his deeper contribution was ensuring that the institution would not depend permanently on its founders. By building both a cultural home and a generation prepared to inherit it, he helped transform immigrant memory into an enduring part of Greater Cleveland.

Mona Alag has spent decades building the informal support systems that helped Cleveland’s growing Indian American community become not only larger, but more connected and better able to care for its own members.

Alag arrived from India on August 17, 1970, as a young newlywed. Cleveland quickly became home. Within only a few months, however, she encountered a side of immigrant life that was rarely visible at cultural celebrations or public gatherings. A woman facing a difficult pregnancy and family crisis approached Alag because she believed she could speak with her confidentially and without judgment.

Alag was only 23, but the experience established a pattern that would continue throughout her life. People began coming to her with family conflicts, relationship problems, health concerns, and difficulties involving their children. Much of her most important work began simply by being someone people trusted enough to call.

Through the Federation of India Community Associations, Alag focused particularly on tensions between immigrant parents and their American-raised children. Working with young people themselves, she organized workshops and seminars intended to help both generations understand the pressures facing the other.

She eventually served on FICA’s Executive Board and as its president for two terms. But some of her most important work took place outside formal leadership positions.

As a founding member of the Association of Asian Indian Women of Ohio, Alag pushed for the creation of a confidential helpline. Its network included professionals such as lawyers, physicians, and social workers who could respond when callers needed more than conversation. Alag recalled taking calls late at night and finding places where she could speak privately in order to protect the caller’s identity.

The helpline addressed a basic problem within a close-knit immigrant community: people sometimes needed help precisely with subjects they were least comfortable discussing publicly. By creating a confidential path to assistance, Alag helped make problems involving family conflict, health, relationships, and other crises easier to confront.

She also became a longtime leader in Project Seva, the service arm of FICA. Its volunteers extended the Indian community’s service beyond itself, preparing meals, distributing blankets and hygiene supplies to Cleveland shelters, knitting blankets for children at Rainbow Babies & Children’s Hospital, and cooking meals for families staying at Ronald McDonald House.

With physicians Dr. Jaya Shah and Dr. Gita Gidwani, Alag later helped establish Helping Hands. The deliberately informal network responded to situations that did not fit neatly within a single institution: domestic violence, immigration problems, terminal illness, legal questions, food assistance, access to public benefits, and temporary housing for people escaping unsafe homes.

Helping Hands also learned how to navigate Cleveland’s larger social-service network. Each case expanded the group’s knowledge of which attorneys, government agencies, nonprofits, healthcare providers, and other resources could respond to particular needs. At times it partnered with Sewa International and other organizations, turning personal relationships into a practical referral network.

Alag’s work also strengthened the cultural side of Indian American life. She chaired KALA, an exhibition showcasing Greater Cleveland Indian artists while raising funds for Family Promise of Greater Cleveland, and participated in programming connected with the India Cultural Garden.

She became an informal ambassador for newcomers as well. Families considering a move to Cleveland or newly settling in the region contacted her with ordinary but important questions: Where should we live? What schools should we consider? Where can we worship? Where can we find familiar food? Who should we call when we need help? By answering those questions, she helped make an unfamiliar city feel navigable.

Underlying all of this work is Alag’s Sikh faith and the principle of *seva*, or selfless service. Her emphasis has often been on helping without public recognition—solving a problem, connecting someone to the right person, raising money, listening to a frightened caller, or quietly making sure that a family has somewhere safe to go.

Mona Alag’s Cleveland legacy is therefore difficult to locate in a single building or position. It exists in the human infrastructure she helped create: a helpline answered in confidence, volunteers serving meals, blankets made for hospitalized children, young people talking with their parents, families escaping violence, artists finding an audience, and newcomers discovering people they could trust. Her work helped turn Cleveland’s Indian American community from a collection of families sharing a heritage into a network capable of supporting people through the realities of everyday life.

Judge Raymond L. “Ray” Pianka spent nearly his entire life in Cleveland’s Detroit Shoreway neighborhood, and that neighborhood became the lens through which he approached community development, City Council, historic preservation, and the law.

Even as a young resident, he organized neighbors to improve the street, including an effort to plant trees whose shade remained decades later. He attended Cleveland public schools and graduated from West High School, where he met his future wife, Karen Olson. He later earned a degree from Cleveland State University and attended Cleveland-Marshall College of Law.

Pianka’s interest in neighborhood organization developed while he was still a student. As a City Council intern, he helped organize block clubs, including an early West 76th Street group, at a time when Detroit Shoreway was losing industrial jobs and experiencing population and property decline.

In 1973, he helped establish the Detroit Shoreway Community Development Organization and became its first executive director. The organization approached neighborhood development as an interconnected problem: housing could not be separated from businesses, jobs, streets, historic buildings, and resident organizations.

One of its defining battles involved the Gordon Square Arcade at West 65th Street and Detroit Avenue. By the late 1970s, the 1920s commercial building had deteriorated so severely that portions of its façade were falling and demolition appeared possible. Pianka, Detroit Shoreway, Our Lady of Mount Carmel, and development partners instead worked to preserve and rehabilitate it. The rescued Arcade later became a central building in the redevelopment of Gordon Square and the surrounding arts district.

Pianka moved from neighborhood organizing into elected office after winning a Cleveland City Council race in 1985. He represented Ward 17 from 1986 through 1995. His neighborhood work continued—one project used federal block-grant money to employ local residents planting trees and improving the I-90 corridor—but his responsibilities became citywide when he chaired Council’s Community and Economic Development Committee.

In that role, Pianka advocated for a more even distribution of federal community-development funding among Cleveland neighborhoods. He also supported stronger building and housing codes and increased resources for building inspections, reflecting his belief that neighborhood stability depended in part on maintaining the city’s existing housing and commercial structures.

In 1995, Pianka was elected judge of Cleveland Municipal Housing Court. He served from 1996 until his death in 2017 and later described the judgeship as the most important and fulfilling form of community service he had undertaken.

His approach reflected what he had learned as a neighborhood organizer. A deteriorated house was not merely an individual parcel: it affected the families next door, the block around it, and ultimately the stability of the neighborhood.

At the same time, Pianka distinguished between different reasons a property might fall into disrepair. An owner-occupant struggling with unemployment, healthcare costs, foreclosure, or limited income presented a different problem from an absentee owner repeatedly ignoring violations.

The Housing Court’s Selective Intervention Program reflected that distinction. First-time owner-occupants cited for code violations could work with Housing Court specialists to establish repair schedules, identify available city, county, and neighborhood resources, and bring their homes into compliance while avoiding a criminal record when the program was successfully completed.

Pianka took a different approach toward owners who repeatedly neglected properties or failed to appear in court. During his tenure, the court used daily fines and other sanctions against noncompliant owners, and Pianka supported remedies that recognized the damage neglected properties could cause surrounding residents. Cleveland City Council later specifically cited those practices when honoring him with the designation Judge Raymond L. Pianka Way.

His knowledge of Cleveland neighborhoods extended far beyond housing codes. Pianka was an avid local historian who could recount the histories of individual buildings, streets, churches, immigrant groups, and families. He helped preserve historic properties in Detroit Shoreway, participated in restoring Fir Street Cemetery, and supported the memorial to Irish American boxing champion Johnny Kilbane. Cleveland Historical now preserves this side of his legacy through a 15-stop Raymond L. Pianka Memorial Walk through Detroit Shoreway.

His Polish heritage was another part of that civic identity. While at Cleveland State, Pianka helped organize Polish American students and supported the study of Polish language and culture. Later, he remained connected with Cleveland Polonia and supported Polish cultural education associated with Slavic Village churches.

But the connection among those places is more important. From block-club organizer to community-development director, councilman, and judge, he consistently treated the condition of Cleveland’s buildings as inseparable from the condition of the communities around them.

Several major events demonstrate that work.

McCall participated in Cleveland’s international effort to secure the 2014 Gay Games, which brought athletes and visitors from around the world to Cleveland and Akron. She later served on the local host organization and represented City Hall in preparations for the event.

In 2016, she helped organize the Cleveland Cavaliers championship parade and served as the City of Cleveland’s lead representative in preparations for the Republican National Convention. In the latter role, her work concerned the practical responsibilities of hosting a National Special Security Event: coordination among governments, transportation agencies, public-safety organizations, businesses, community groups, communications teams, and other partners.

Transportation became a second major arena for her public service. McCall joined the Greater Cleveland Regional Transit Authority Board in 2006. She chaired committees involving planning, development, safety, and security and worked with RTA on transportation planning for major Cleveland events. Her board service continued until May 2023.

Her transit work eventually reached the national level. After serving as vice chair, McCall became Chair of the American Public Transportation Association for 2015–2016, representing an industry encompassing bus, rail, paratransit, and other public transportation systems throughout North America. The American Public Transportation Foundation later established the Valarie J. McCall Scholarship in recognition of that service.

She also participated in regional transportation and infrastructure planning through the Northeast Ohio Areawide Coordinating Agency, including service as president of its governing board. Her involvement connected decisions about transit with larger questions of regional development, environmental planning, transportation funding, and access.

Another strand of McCall’s career connected Cleveland with the world. As the city’s principal representative in Sister Cities relationships, she worked with international partners on exchanges involving government, education, culture, business, and professional life. Programs with Cleveland sister cities such as Rouen, France, brought that diplomacy down to a human scale through exchanges among students, professionals, civic leaders, and even chefs.

Her international-affairs work also intersected with Cleveland’s own immigrant and nationality communities. During her City Hall years, ethnic organizations came to know McCall as an official who helped make municipal spaces—including the City Hall Rotunda—available for heritage celebrations and public cultural events.

Cleveland State University awarded McCall an Honorary Doctor of Public Service in 2012. After leaving City Hall at the end of the Jackson administration, she continued her work through the Valarie McCall Consulting Agency.

Valarie McCall’s Cleveland legacy is unusually visible in the connections between things: a bus ride and access to work; a neighborhood and federal investment; City Hall and an ethnic celebration; Cleveland and a sister city overseas; or a major public event and the transportation, government, nonprofit, business, and community networks required to make it happen.

Across those roles, her contribution was often the work between institutions—turning policy, partnerships, and civic relationships into opportunities that Cleveland residents could actually encounter.

Georgine Welo has spent much of her life keeping institutions alive—first within Greater Cleveland’s Serbian American community and later as an elected leader in one of Cleveland’s inner-ring suburbs.

Born in Cleveland in 1958, Welo was raised in a family where Serbian Orthodox church life was part of everyday life. At St. Sava Serbian Orthodox Cathedral in Parma, she attended cultural classes and Sunday School, read the Epistle, worked church banquets, washed dishes alongside other volunteers, and eventually became a Sunday School teacher.

That participation followed her to the University of Akron. Welo remained active in Serbian choir, church, folk dance, lodge activities, and athletic events and traveled with Serbian singers to communities throughout the United States and Canada. In 1977, she was selected as Miss Njegosh, reflecting a connection to the Serbian Singing Federation that would become a major part of her adult life.

When Welo returned to Cleveland in 1978, she immediately helped restart the S.S.S. Njegosh Choir. She recruited relatives, friends, fellow parishioners, and her future husband, Carter Welo, into the group and later served as its president.

Around the same time, another important Serbian institution needed help. The Serbian Orthodox Diocese had regained Shadeland, its camp in Pennsylvania, but the property was in poor condition. Welo and her husband organized friends in the building trades, recruited volunteers, coordinated materials, and raised money. Weekend crews repaired and repainted the grounds so Shadeland could reopen that summer. It went on to become a major Serbian Orthodox summer camp serving later generations of families.

Welo repeatedly took on the practical work required to keep cultural institutions functioning. At St. Sava Cathedral, she served on the board and as assistant treasurer, helped oversee projects including air conditioning and improvements to the parish home, and became Sunday School superintendent. She produced the weekly parish bulletin and edited the quarterly *St. Sava Herald*, working to make church and cultural information available in both Serbian and English.

She also helped bring Serbian culture into Cleveland’s larger public celebrations. For years, Welo chaired the Serbian booth at the Cleveland Nationality Festival on Mall C, organizing food, volunteers, and entertainment. In 1983, she chaired a major Serbian Singing Federation festival hosted by St. Sava and the Njegosh Choir; Cleveland Mayor George Voinovich marked the occasion by proclaiming May 28 Serbian Singing Society Day.

As the city’s older nationality festivals evolved into new forms, Welo continued participating. Through the Serbian Cultural Garden and One World Day, she helped present Serbian music, dance, food, faith, and history within Cleveland’s larger multicultural landscape. At One World Day in 2019, she served as Mistress of Ceremonies for a naturalization program hosted by the Serbian Cultural Garden.

Youth remained central to her work. Welo taught Sunday School, supported dance, choir, sports, and cultural programs, and encouraged younger participants to assume responsibility for institutions created by earlier immigrant generations. During a visit to Serbia, she also brought art supplies to students at Svetozar Marković School in Subotica so they could create work reflecting their Serbian heritage.

Her community leadership eventually expanded into municipal government.

After moving to South Euclid with Carter in 1979 and helping with the family hardware business, Welo became involved in neighborhood and municipal organizations. She served on South Euclid City Council from 1992 to 1998, including time as Council President Pro Tem, later worked as an administrative bailiff in Cuyahoga County Common Pleas Court, and served on municipal planning and zoning bodies.

In November 2003, voters elected Welo as South Euclid’s first woman mayor. She took office on January 1, 2004 and remains mayor in 2026. Her tenure has placed her at the center of an inner-ring suburb confronting issues familiar across Greater Cleveland: aging housing, changing demographics, commercial redevelopment, vacant properties, transportation, environmental planning, and the need to retain residents while attracting new ones.

Her regional service has extended through organizations concerned with public transit, energy, watershed management, planning, first-ring suburbs, aging, and intergovernmental cooperation. She has served in leadership or board roles with organizations including the First Suburbs Consortium, NOPEC, Greater Cleveland RTA, Euclid Creek Watershed Council, and regional mayors' and planning organizations.

The connection between these two sides of Welo’s life is unusually direct. The skills required to keep a choir active, repair a summer camp, organize hundreds of festival volunteers, publish a bilingual church bulletin, or persuade young people to participate are also skills of local government: coordinating people, maintaining institutions, responding to changing needs, and creating reasons for residents to remain invested in a place.

Georgine Welo’s Greater Cleveland legacy therefore extends from St. Sava Cathedral and the Njegosh Choir to One World Day and South Euclid City Hall. Across those settings, her work has centered on the everyday labor through which communities endure—maintaining their institutions while making room for the people who will inherit them.

Ambassador Edward F. Crawford built companies from Cleveland that eventually operated around the world, then used that success to strengthen educational, medical, cultural, and Irish American institutions throughout Northeast Ohio.

Crawford’s own Cleveland story began almost by accident. In 1948, his parents were moving their family west toward California when their vehicle broke down while crossing Ohio. Instead of continuing west, the family settled in Cleveland Heights. The decision established the home base from which Crawford would later build businesses, raise a family, participate in civic life, and reconnect publicly with his family’s Irish roots.

His grandparents had emigrated from County Cork, and their immigrant experience remained an important part of Crawford’s understanding of family and opportunity.

After serving in the Ohio Army National Guard, Crawford entered manufacturing. In 1962, while still attending college classes at night, he became President and CEO of Cleveland Steel Container. His career subsequently included other manufacturing businesses and the creation of The Crawford Group, but his largest expansion began with Park-Ohio in 1992.

Crawford pursued growth through more than 100 business transactions, transforming Park-Ohio from a relatively small Cleveland manufacturer into an international industrial, manufacturing, and supply-chain corporation. Under his leadership, the publicly traded company grew to approximately $1.6 billion in business, employing more than 7,000 people at 125 locations worldwide.

That business career increasingly supported a parallel life of civic involvement. Crawford served or supported institutions including John Carroll University, Cleveland Clinic’s Hillcrest Hospital, Ronald McDonald House, Our Lady of the Wayside, Kent State University, and organizations concerned with healthcare, education, military families, and community service.

One of his most visible contributions began with a drive along Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard.

Crawford remembered Cleveland’s Cultural Gardens from his youth and was disturbed by the deteriorated condition of the Irish Cultural Garden. After seeing volunteers working there, he began contacting friends and other Irish American leaders. In 2007, that effort led to the formation of the Irish Garden Club, created specifically to raise money and organize the Garden’s restoration.

The project drew together a network of Cleveland Irish civic leaders, including Jack Kahl, Sheila Murphy Crawford, Martin Keane, Martin Sweeney, and others. Rather than allowing a historic ethnic landmark to continue deteriorating, the group repaired landscaping, restored features, added monuments, and raised substantial private support. The four-acre Irish Cultural Garden was formally rededicated in October 2009.

Crawford also pursued additions that connected Cleveland physically with Ireland. During a business trip to Dublin, he admired a fountain associated with St. Patrick’s Cathedral and returned determined to create a comparable feature in Cleveland. With support from the Fred Lennon Foundation, the fountain became a centerpiece of the restored Garden.

The revitalized garden became not simply a memorial to Irish heritage but an active civic gathering place. In 2012, Crawford hosted Taoiseach Enda Kenny, Ireland’s head of government, along with Irish diplomatic officials at the Garden—an early example of how Crawford’s Cleveland Irish involvement increasingly crossed into international relations.

That connection reached its highest public level in 2019, when Crawford became U.S. Ambassador to the Republic of Ireland. He served in Dublin from 2019 to 2021. The appointment transformed a relationship with Ireland that had begun with family memory and Cleveland cultural preservation into formal diplomatic service between the two countries.

While serving in Ireland, Crawford also created the ASPIRE Entrepreneurial Workshop Series, drawing on his own experience of building companies to mentor entrepreneurs. The program later became part of another major Northeast Ohio institution: Kent State University.

In 2021, Crawford and his family provided the largest single philanthropic gift in Kent State history. The contribution allowed the university to complete the campaign for a new business-school building and resulted in the naming of the Ambassador Crawford College of Business and Entrepreneurship and Crawford Hall. The new building opened in 2024 with classrooms, entrepreneurship and business-analytics facilities, research spaces, a trading lab, and student-support areas.

Crawford’s involvement with the university has continued. Kent State appointed him a National Trustee in 2022 and reappointed him to a second term beginning in 2025. He also remains active in business as Chairman of Crawford United and through The Crawford Group.

Ambassador Edward Crawford’s Cleveland legacy can therefore be seen in several kinds of institutions. He built manufacturing companies that carried a Cleveland enterprise into global markets. He helped rescue an Irish Cultural Garden that physically preserves immigrant memory within the city. And he turned business success into educational infrastructure that will serve generations of Northeast Ohio students.

Across those efforts, the common thread is institution-building: creating businesses, restoring cultural places, supporting civic organizations, and investing in universities so that the structures connecting one generation to the next remain strong.

Branka M. Malinar has spent her life making memory tangible. In Northeast Ohio, she built educational programs for children, helped restore a nineteenth-century community theater, founded historical institutions, developed museum collections, and helped create a permanent public place for Croatian heritage in Cleveland’s Cultural Gardens.

Born in Popovec, Croatia, in 1941, Malinar was four when her family fled the postwar Communist takeover of Yugoslavia. They escaped first to Austria, where they spent two years in a displaced-persons camp, and later moved to Munich, Germany. In 1951, the family crossed the Atlantic aboard the *S.S. General Muir*, arriving at Ellis Island on May 17. With assistance from a family sponsoring them through Catholic Charities, they settled in Cleveland.

Malinar was ten years old and already spoke three languages.

In Cleveland, she attended St. Paul’s Croatian Elementary School and Notre Dame Academy. Her education took place alongside an active Croatian cultural life: as a young woman she taught Croatian folk dancing to children for six years and performed with the UAC KOLO Dancers. Through the dance group she met Jerry Malinar, whom she married in 1961.

Malinar initially studied chemistry at Flora Stone Mather College of Western Reserve University. After she and Jerry moved to North Ridgeville in 1968 with their growing family, education became her profession. While raising four daughters—Drina, Mirna, Vesna, and Nada—she participated in the local PTA, served as a Girl Scout leader, and worked as a library assistant.

In 1973, Malinar completed a degree in elementary education at Baldwin Wallace College and began teaching math and science in North Ridgeville City Schools. She later earned a master’s degree from Cleveland State University in curriculum and gifted education.

When the district needed a program for gifted students, Malinar was asked to create it. She developed the curriculum and taught students across three grade levels for the next 22 years.

Her classroom became only one part of her educational work. She coordinated Science Olympiad competitions, introduced students to astronomy through Star Lab, served for six years as computer coordinator at Wilcox Elementary, and directed the district’s Young Authors Program for 18 years. The Ohio Association of Gifted Coordinators named her Northeast Ohio Teacher of the Year.

Malinar’s belief in education also extended beyond schools.

In 1976, she joined a group of North Ridgeville residents seeking to rescue the unused second-floor theater inside the city’s historic Old Town Hall. Built in 1882–1883, the building had served generations of residents before municipal offices moved elsewhere in 1975. Its upstairs opera hall still contained a stage and rows of old theater seats but required extensive restoration.

Malinar chaired the restoration committee. Volunteers sanded the seats, repaired and painted walls, raised money, and gradually returned the abandoned space to use. After presenting performances elsewhere while construction continued, the group opened its restored theater in September 1977 with a production of *Little Women*. The project became the Olde Towne Hall Theatre.

That preservation effort soon expanded downstairs. In 1977, Branka and Jerry joined other residents in founding the North Ridgeville Historical Society. The Society eventually established its museum in the first floor of the same Old Town Hall, preserving photographs, documents, artifacts, and other evidence of the community’s history.

At the same time, Malinar was preserving another history: the Croatian immigrant experience that had brought her own family to Cleveland.

In 1983, Branka and Jerry became founding members of the American Croatian Lodge in Eastlake. One of the Lodge’s major projects became the Croatian Heritage Museum and Library. Malinar helped develop its collections and library, organize exhibitions, write grants and fundraising appeals, and turn donated objects into educational resources capable of telling Croatian stories to later generations. The museum remains active in Eastlake.

In 2009, the Malinars joined the group developing the Croatian Cultural Garden in Cleveland’s Rockefeller Park. The project translated the same preservation work into public space, using landscape, sculpture, art, and cultural programming to make Croatian history visible within Cleveland’s larger collection of nationality gardens.

Malinar also preserved the immigrant experience nationally. In 1993, she recorded her story for the Ellis Island Oral History Project, ensuring that researchers and future visitors could hear a firsthand account of displacement, refugee camps, migration, and settlement in Cleveland.

More than two decades later, she returned another part of her family history to Ellis Island. In 2016, she donated two Croatian folk costumes and a handmade towel, accompanied by information explaining how the garments were made and a biography of her father, Nikola Frigan. Objects that had once belonged to one immigrant family became part of the public record of American immigration.

Her work also continued inside her own family. Beginning in 2006, Malinar drove two of her grandchildren every week to American Zagreb Junior Tamburitzans rehearsals, where they learned Croatian instrumental music, singing, and dance. She made that trip for seven years.

That detail captures the continuity running through her career. Whether she was designing lessons for gifted students, restoring an old theater, cataloging a museum object, recording an oral history, writing a Cultural Garden grant, or taking grandchildren to tamburitza lessons, Malinar treated preservation as a form of education.

Branka Malinar’s Northeast Ohio legacy therefore exists in both people and places: students challenged by programs she created, audiences inside a theater residents rescued, artifacts preserved in museums, Croatian history represented in Rockefeller Park, and descendants given opportunities to understand the experiences that brought their families to Cleveland.

Her work made memory something people could enter, handle, study, perform, and pass on.
