Aklilu Demessie has spent more than five decades turning opportunities he first received as a young Ethiopian exchange student into opportunities for others—through engineering, education, immigrant organizations, humanitarian work, and international relationships centered in Cleveland.

Demessie first came to Ohio from Ethiopia in the early 1970s through the American Field Service exchange program. As a senior from Menelik High School in Addis Ababa, he lived with a host family in Oberlin and graduated from Oberlin High School in 1971. The experience immersed him in American family and community life and established a relationship with Ohio that would shape the rest of his life.

After the exchange year, Demessie returned to Ethiopia and enrolled at Haile Selassie University, now Addis Ababa University. His studies were interrupted after his first semester when the university was closed amid a major student movement for political reform. He returned to Ohio and enrolled at Case Western Reserve University, earning a B.S. in structural and civil engineering and an M.S. in engineering mechanics.

Cleveland then became the base of a 44-year aerospace career.

Demessie began at Cleveland Pneumatic Company as a stress analyst and advanced into engineering supervision. He later worked as a senior engineer, group leader, and supervisor with Goodrich Landing Gear and its successor aerospace businesses, specializing in aircraft landing-gear structures and materials for military and commercial aviation. He retired from United Technologies Aerospace Systems in 2018, consulted with Collins Aerospace for another three years, and permanently retired from aerospace in 2021.

He treated engineering as an educational responsibility as well as a profession. Demessie trained younger engineers entering his workplace, mentored co-op students, and advised high-school and college students interested in technical careers. He also helped connect his employer’s resources with educational needs abroad, including coordinating the donation of 40 computers to Addis Ababa University and helping send books, educational materials, and medical supplies to Ethiopia.

At the same time, Demessie became one of the organizers helping Cleveland’s growing Ethiopian community build durable institutions.

He served as president of the Northeast Ohio Ethiopian Community Association and the Ethiopian Cleveland Connection. He was also one of five original founders of the Society of Ethiopians Established in the Diaspora, or SEED. After approximately 25 years as the organization’s secretary, he became its president.

His civic work increasingly connected Cleveland directly with Ethiopia.

As a longtime board member and vice president of the Menelik Foundation, Demessie was part of the group that established the Sister City relationship between Cleveland and Bahir Dar, Ethiopia, in 2004. The agreement created a formal framework for cultural, educational, civic, and people-to-people relationships between the two cities.

That same year, Cleveland hosted the International Children’s Games. Demessie traveled to Ethiopia to recruit young athletes from Bahir Dar to participate. Their arrival made Ethiopia the first African nation represented in the Cleveland Games, turning an international sporting event into a direct connection between young people in the two sister cities.

Demessie also helped make Ethiopian identity physically visible within Cleveland.

As a member of the design committee for the Ethiopian Cultural Garden, he participated in developing a permanent site within Rockefeller Park representing Ethiopian history and culture. His Hall of Fame biography identifies it as the first Ethiopian Cultural Garden established outside Ethiopia. He also served on the Cleveland Cultural Gardens Federation board.

His international work extended across Cleveland’s many nationality communities. Demessie has been involved with the International Community Council–Worldwide Intercultural Network, or ICC-WIN, since the 1990s and now serves as a vice president. The organization connects representatives from more than 100 national backgrounds, giving his Ethiopian civic work a place within Cleveland’s larger multicultural network.

Humanitarian service developed alongside those cultural relationships. During periods of famine in Ethiopia, Demessie helped connect Cleveland churches and community organizations with relief efforts. Through the Menelik Foundation, he also participated in sending more than 150 cots, blankets, and other supplies to Hurricane Katrina survivors in Louisiana in 2005.

Education remained one of his most consistent priorities. With his longtime friend Dr. Shiferaw Gebre-Mariam, Demessie helped build the DISATU EYES Foundation, which supports high-potential Ethiopian girls through educational assistance, STEM tutoring, and healthcare initiatives. The project extends a principle that runs through his own biography: access to education can alter the direction of an entire life.

He has also remained active with St. Mary Ethiopian Orthodox Church in Cleveland, serving in advisory and organizational roles and adding faith institutions to the network of community organizations he helped sustain.

The exchange experience that first brought Demessie to Ohio never disappeared from his thinking. Decades later, he joined other Ethiopian AFS alumni and advocated for renewed educational exchange between Ethiopia and the United States. In that sense, his civic career repeatedly returned to the opportunity that shaped his own life: allowing a young person to encounter another place, another community, and possibilities that might otherwise have remained inaccessible.

Aklilu Demessie’s Cleveland legacy lies in building those pathways. From Case Western Reserve laboratories and aerospace engineering departments to Ethiopian community associations, the Cultural Gardens, Cleveland’s Sister Cities network, student exchanges, and classrooms in Ethiopia, he has repeatedly connected technical knowledge, cultural identity, and civic relationships.

His work demonstrates how one international student’s experience in Ohio could grow into a lifetime of creating connections between Cleveland and the wider world.
